tldr: An efficient quantum algorithm for the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem unifies key symmetry-learning primitives.
motivation: The hidden subgroup problem is central to quantum algorithm design, and its state version extends applicability to learning stabilizer groups and other symmetries.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that solves the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem by leveraging Fourier sampling and group-theoretic techniques.
result: The algorithm efficiently learns stabilizer groups and other Abelian hidden subgroups, unifying several symmetry-learning tasks.
conclusion: This work provides a unified framework for symmetry learning in quantum information, with implications for quantum algorithms and complexity theory.

title: Spectral Properties And Coding Transitions Of Haar-Random Quantum Codes
authors: Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, And Sarang Gopalakrishnan
abstract:
Author(s): Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, and Sarang Gopalakrishnan

An investigation of Haar-random quantum codes reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and nondecodable phases of quantum codes under local noise.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020328] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates Haar-random quantum codes and reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and non-decodable phases under local noise.
motivation: Understanding the robustness of quantum error-correcting codes against local noise is crucial for practical quantum computing. The paper aims to characterize the spectral properties and coding transitions of random quantum codes.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random quantum codes using statistical physics methods, studying the spectral properties of the code's density matrix and the behavior of the coherent information under local noise.
result: They identify a sharp transition between decodable and non-decodable phases, with the transition point determined by the code rate and noise strength. The spectral properties exhibit universal features near the transition.
conclusion: The work provides a simple mechanism for the decoding transition in random quantum codes, offering insights into the design of practical quantum error-correcting codes.

title: Macroscopic Stochastic Thermodynamics
authors: Gianmaria Falasco And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Author(s): Gianmaria Falasco and Massimiliano Esposito

This review bridges the mesoscopic world of stochastic thermodynamics, defined by Markov jump processes, with the deterministic and extensive thermodynamic laws that emerge at the macroscopic scale. Using large deviations theory, it constructs a fluctuation framework preserving core principles like the fluctuation theorem. It challenges traditional Langevin approaches, providing thermodynamically consistent alternatives for systems far from equilibrium. From chemical reaction networks to electronic circuits and Potts models, this work elucidates the dynamics of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production principles, offering a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015002] Published Wed Jan 22, 2025.
tldr: A review bridging stochastic thermodynamics at the mesoscopic scale with macroscopic thermodynamic laws using large deviations theory.
motivation: To provide a thermodynamically consistent framework for nonequilibrium systems that goes beyond traditional Langevin approaches.
method: Uses large deviations theory to construct a fluctuation framework for Markov jump processes, preserving fluctuation theorems and entropy production principles.
result: Establishes a robust theoretical foundation for understanding rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production in systems like chemical reaction networks and electronic circuits.
conclusion: The framework offers a unified description of nonequilibrium phenomena across scales, challenging conventional methods and providing new insights.

title: Entanglement In The Dicke Subspace
authors: Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, And Clément Pellegrini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2150 (2026).

We provide a complete mathematical theory for the entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states. These quantum states form an important subclass of bosonic states arising in the study of indistinguishable particles. We introduce a tensor-based parametrization where the diagonal entries of these states are encoded as a symmetric tensor, enabling a direct translation between entanglement properties and well-studied convex cones of tensors. Our results bridge multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and the theory of completely positive and copositive tensors. This dictionary maps separability to completely positive tensors, the PPT property to moment tensors, entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors, and decomposable witnesses to sum of squares tensors. We establish that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension [MATH] and [MATH] parties, disproving a recent conjecture. We also show that, for mixtures of Dicke states, the PPT condition with respect to the most balanced bipartition implies all other PPT conditions. We further connect bosonic extendibility of mixtures of Dicke states to the duals of known hierarchies for non-negative polynomials, such as the ones by Reznick and Polya. We thus provide semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

.
tldr: Provides a complete mathematical theory for entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states, linking separability to completely positive tensors and PPT property to moment tensors.
motivation: To develop a unified framework for understanding entanglement in the important subclass of Dicke states, which arise in bosonic systems.
method: Introduces a tensor-based parametrization where diagonal entries are encoded as symmetric tensors, mapping entanglement properties to convex cones of tensors.
result: Establishes existence of PPT entanglement for all multipartite systems with local dimension ≥3 and ≥3 parties, disproving a recent conjecture; shows PPT condition for most balanced bipartition implies all others.
conclusion: Provides semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace, bridging multipartite entanglement with semialgebraic geometry.

title: Measuring Rényi Entropy With An Echo Protocol
authors: Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, And Julian Sonner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2146 (2026).

We present efficient and practical protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy, whose exponential is known as the purity. Our approach is based on expressing the purity in terms of transition probabilities generated by an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, making it applicable to quantum many-body systems. Notably, our approach does not rely on random-noise averaging, a feature that can be extended to protocols to measure out-of-time-order correlation functions, as we demonstrate. By way of example, we show that our protocols can be practically implemented in superconducting qubit-based platforms, as well as in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.

.
tldr: Presents efficient echo-based protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy (purity) in quantum many-body systems without random-noise averaging.
motivation: Measuring Rényi entropy is crucial for characterizing entanglement and quantum correlations, but existing methods often require random averaging or are inefficient.
method: The purity is expressed in terms of transition probabilities from an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, avoiding random-noise averaging; the protocol is extended to out-of-time-order correlators.
result: The protocols are shown to be practically implementable on superconducting qubit platforms and in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.
conclusion: The work provides efficient, noise-avoiding measurement schemes for Rényi entropy, advancing experimental quantum information processing.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: Tight bounds on the query complexity of quantum phase estimation with advice states, resolving open problems and providing matching upper and lower bounds.
motivation: Phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine, but its cost when given imperfect advice (states with partial overlap with the top eigenspace) was not well understood. The authors aim to characterize the optimal trade-offs.
method: The paper uses the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials to derive lower bounds, and constructs explicit algorithms that nearly match these bounds for all parameter regimes.
result: They show that a small number of advice copies are not significantly better than no advice, and that many copies do not drastically reduce cost. They also prove a tight bound for error probability reduction in basic phase estimation.
conclusion: The work provides a nearly complete characterization of phase estimation complexity under advice, and resolves an open question on the unitary recurrence time problem.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity, showing that stabilizer states maximally violate it and linking Bell violation to Wigner negativity volume.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because known qubit results do not extend directly; this work aims to connect nonlocality to Wigner negativity in qudits.
method: Introduces a new CHSH-like inequality for qudits using correlations derived from Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized Hadamard gate; analyzes the Bell operator's relation to singlet fraction and Wigner negativity volume.
result: A specific stabilizer state achieves maximal violation among all qudit states, and the Bell operator quantifies both singlet fraction and Wigner negativity volume; rational-phase diagonal unitaries reproduce CGLMP and SATWAP violations.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems, and the proposed inequality provides a direct link between nonlocality and a quantum resource theory.

title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a quantum walk on simplicial complexes that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, enabling superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: Quantum walks on graphs have shown advantages, but extending them to simplicial complexes could unlock new quantum algorithms for topological data analysis and homology computation.
method: The authors construct a unitary encoding of the combinatorial Laplacian using a quantum walk on oriented simplices, with coherent interference between positive and negative orientations to encode the Laplacian. They also build variant walks for persistent Betti numbers, QMA-hard problems, and the high-dimensional Dirichlet problem.
result: The quantum walk achieves an apparent superpolynomial speedup over classical algorithms for estimating Betti numbers and solving the high-dimensional Dirichlet problem, assuming an inverse-polynomial spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: Quantum walks on simplicial complexes provide a powerful framework for topological data analysis and computational topology, with potential exponential advantages in certain regimes.

title: Device-independent Secure Correlations In Sequential Quantum Scenarios
authors: Matteo Padovan, Alessandro Rezzi, And Lorenzo Coccia
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2131 (2026).

Device-independent quantum information is attracting significant attention, particularly for its applications in information security. This interest arises because the security of device-independent protocols relies solely on the observed outcomes of spatially separated measurements and the validity of quantum physics. Sequential scenarios, i.e., where measurements occur in a precise temporal order, have been proved to enhance performance of device-independent protocols in some specific cases by enabling the reuse of the same quantum state. In this work, we propose a systematic approach to designing sequential quantum protocols for device-independent security. Our method begins with a bipartite self-testing qubit protocol and transforms it into a sequential protocol by replacing one measurement with its non-projective counterpart and adding an additional user thereafter. We analytically prove that, with this systematic construction, the resulting ideal correlations are secure in the sense that they cannot be reproduced as a statistical mixture of other correlations, thereby enabling, for example, the device-independent certification of all the randomness present in the observed correlations. The general recipe we provide can be exploited for further development of new device-independent quantum schemes for security.

.
tldr: A systematic method to construct device-independent secure sequential quantum protocols from bipartite self-testing qubit protocols.
motivation: Sequential scenarios can enhance device-independent protocols by reusing quantum states, but a general construction method was lacking.
method: Replace one measurement in a bipartite self-testing qubit protocol with a non-projective measurement and add an additional user, then prove security analytically.
result: The resulting ideal correlations are secure against statistical mixture reproduction, enabling device-independent certification of randomness.
conclusion: The recipe provides a systematic way to develop new device-independent quantum security schemes in sequential scenarios.

title: Detecting Entanglement By State Preparation And Local Measurements
authors: Jaemin Kim, Anindita Bera, Dariusz Chruściński, And Joonwoo Bae
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2128 (2026).

Entanglement witnesses (EWs) are a collection of observables that can characterize separable states and, experimentally, estimating EWs can verify entangled states. In this work, we show that a fixed measurement setting on a multipartite entangled state, which we introduce as a network state for the purpose, can estimate EWs. Namely, entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner, in which experimenters do not necessarily change measurement settings. We present a fixed measurement setting and network states for estimating decomposable EWs, equivalent to the partial transpose criteria. We also consider non-decomposable EWs that detect bound entangled states beyond the partial transpose criteria. The results can be extended to multipartite states such as graph states, a resource for measurement-based quantum computing, and readily applied to distributed settings such as quantum metrology or sensor networks where multipartite entangled states are resourceful.

.
tldr: This paper shows that a fixed measurement setting on a multipartite network state can estimate entanglement witnesses, enabling measurement-based entanglement verification without changing measurement settings.
motivation: Entanglement witnesses are crucial for detecting entanglement, but typically require changing measurement settings. The authors aim to simplify experimental verification by using a fixed measurement setting.
method: The authors introduce a network state and a fixed measurement setting to estimate decomposable and non-decomposable entanglement witnesses, including those for bound entangled states. They extend the method to multipartite graph states.
result: They demonstrate that entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner without changing measurement settings, and the method applies to multipartite states and distributed settings.
conclusion: The work provides a practical approach for entanglement detection that is resource-efficient and applicable to quantum networks and metrology.

title: A Local Automaton For The 2d Toric Code
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, And Ethan Lake
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2125 (2026).

We construct a local decoder for the 2D toric code using ideas from the hierarchical classical cellular automata of Tsirelson and Gács. Our decoder is a circuit of strictly local quantum operations preserving a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without the need for non-local classical computation or communication. Our construction is not translation invariant in spacetime, but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes. This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.

.
tldr: Constructs a local decoder for the 2D toric code that preserves a logical state for exponential time using hierarchical cellular automata, solving the open problem of a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.
motivation: Topological quantum memories require decoders that are both local and fault-tolerant; previous constructions required non-local classical processing or higher dimensions.
method: The decoder is built from strictly local quantum operations inspired by Tsirelson and Gács's hierarchical classical cellular automata, and is not translation invariant in spacetime but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacked toric codes.
result: The decoder maintains a logical state for exponential time under circuit-level noise without non-local classical computation or communication.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that a local topological quantum memory is possible in 2D, advancing the theory of quantum error correction and fault tolerance.

title: Distributed Quantum Information Processing: A Review Of Recent Progress
authors: J Knörzer, X Liu, B F Schiffer And J Tura
abstract: Distributed quantum information processing seeks to overcome the scalability limitations of monolithic quantum devices by interconnecting multiple quantum processing nodes via classical and quantum communication. This approach extends the capabilities of individual devices, enabling access to larger problem instances and novel algorithmic techniques. Beyond increasing qubit counts, it also enables qualitatively new capabilities, such as joint measurements on multiple copies of high-dimensional quantum states. The distinction between single-copy and multi-copy access reveals important differences in task complexity and helps identify which computational problems stand to benefit from distributed quantum resources. At the same time, it highlights trade-offs between classical and quantum communication models and the practical challenges involved in realizing them experimentally. In this review, we contextualize recent developments by surveying the theoretical foundations of distributed quantum protocols and examining the experimental platforms and algorithmic applications that realize them in practice.
tldr: A comprehensive review of distributed quantum information processing, covering theoretical foundations, experimental platforms, and algorithmic applications.
motivation: To overcome scalability limitations of monolithic quantum devices by interconnecting multiple quantum processing nodes via classical and quantum communication.
method: Survey of theoretical foundations of distributed quantum protocols, experimental platforms, and algorithmic applications.
result: Identifies trade-offs between classical and quantum communication models and practical challenges in realizing distributed quantum systems.
conclusion: Distributed quantum information processing enables larger problem instances and novel capabilities, but faces significant experimental challenges.

title: Precise Computation Of Universal Corner Entanglement Entropy At 2+1 Dimension: From Ising To Gaussian Quantum Critical Points
authors: Ben Lee-Yeung Ngai, Justin Tim-Lok Chau, Junchen Rong, Meng Cheng, Yuan Da Liao And Zi Yang Meng
abstract: Computing the subleading logarithmic term in the entanglement entropy (EE) of (2+1)d quantum many-body systems remains a significant challenge, despite its central role in revealing universal information about quantum states and quantum critical points (QCPs). Building on recent algorithmic advances that enable the stable calculation of EE as an exponential observable (Zhou et al 2024 Phys. Rev. B109 165106; Zhang et al 2024 Phys. Rev. B109 205147; Liao et al 2024 Phys. Rev. B110 235111), we develop a bubble basis projector quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) algorithm to precisely and efficiently compute the universal corner of EE at QCPs in a (2+1)d square-lattice transverse-field Ising model augmented with a four-body interaction. Turning on this interaction allows us to trace an Ising critical line, reaching the tricritical point, and then a line of first-order phase transition. In (2+1)d, the tricritical point is described by the Gaussian theory, where a theoretical calculation of the corner logarithmic term in the 2nd Rényi entropy term is available (Casini and Huerta 2007 Nucl. Phys. B764 183). Our QMC results are in quantitative agreement with this theoretical value, providing a highly nontrivial benchmark of the algorithm. Furthermore, we also study the Rényi EE at the Ising critical line and on the first-order transition line, obtaining results consistent with theoretical expectations. These findings establish the long-sought connection between the universal values of an exactly solvable limit and those of a strongly correlated regime at (2+1)d.
tldr: This paper computes the universal corner entanglement entropy at (2+1)d quantum critical points using a novel QMC algorithm, achieving quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions.
motivation: Computing subleading logarithmic terms in entanglement entropy for (2+1)d systems is challenging but crucial for revealing universal information about quantum states and critical points.
method: The authors develop a bubble basis projector quantum Monte Carlo algorithm to compute the 2nd Rényi entropy as an exponential observable, applied to a square-lattice transverse-field Ising model with a four-body interaction.
result: The QMC results for the corner logarithmic term at the Gaussian tricritical point match the theoretical value from Casini and Huerta, and results at the Ising critical line and first-order transition line are consistent with expectations.
conclusion: The algorithm establishes a connection between universal values in exactly solvable limits and strongly correlated regimes, providing a benchmark for future studies of entanglement entropy in (2+1)d.

title: Fault-tolerant Quantum Computation With Static Atomic Buses
authors: Matteo Bergonzoni, Laura Pecorari, Sam Norrell, Cody Poole, Guido Pupillo, Mark Saffman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing require scalable, high-fidelity long-range connectivity. In neutral-atom quantum computers, this is commonly achieved through atom transport, but shuttling introduces latency and motional heating that worsen with system size. Here, we introduce a neutral-atom architecture based on static atomic buses, in which auxiliary mediator atoms enable long-range entangling operations without qubit transport. The architecture naturally supports long-range stabilizer measurements in high-rate LDPC codes and transversal logical gates between neighboring surface-code patches, enabling a modular framework for efficient logical memories, Clifford computation, and magic-state distillation. To realize these capabilities, we co-design optimal-control protocols for bus-mediated controlled-Z gates that incorporate both microscopic neutral-atom dynamics and architectural constraints. We obtain smooth bus-mediated gates with fidelities approaching 99.9% and durations of a few hundred nanoseconds by combining time-optimal control with interaction-flatness and robustness constraints. Large-scale simulations of quantum error correction and logical entangling operations between neighboring surface-code patches predict more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in logical error rates compared with atom-shuttling architectures under realistic noise. The architecture achieves logical gate times of approximately 100 us and quantum-error-correction cycle times of about 1 ms for code distances d<12. These results establish static atomic buses as a practical alternative to atom shuttling for scalable fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing.
tldr: Proposes a neutral-atom quantum computing architecture using static atomic buses for long-range entangling gates without atom shuttling, enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation with improved logical error rates.
motivation: Atom shuttling in neutral-atom quantum computers introduces latency and motional heating that limit scalability. The authors aim to provide an alternative architecture that supports long-range connectivity for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: They introduce static atomic buses where auxiliary mediator atoms enable long-range entangling operations. Co-designed optimal-control protocols for bus-mediated controlled-Z gates incorporate microscopic dynamics and architectural constraints.
result: Bus-mediated gates achieve fidelities approaching 99.9% with durations of a few hundred nanoseconds. Large-scale simulations show more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in logical error rates compared to atom-shuttling architectures.
conclusion: Static atomic buses offer a practical alternative to atom shuttling for scalable fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing, with logical gate times of ~100 μs and QEC cycle times of ~1 ms for code distances d<12.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel neutral-atom quantum computing architecture based on static atomic buses, where auxiliary mediator atoms facilitate long-range entangling operations without the need for physical qubit transport. The architecture eliminates the latency and motional heating associated with atom shuttling, which becomes increasingly problematic as system size grows. The authors co-design optimal-control protocols for bus-mediated controlled-Z (CZ) gates, achieving fidelities approaching 99.9% with durations of a few hundred nanoseconds by incorporating time-optimal control, interaction-flatness, and robustness constraints. The architecture naturally supports long-range stabilizer measurements in high-rate LDPC codes and transversal logical gates between neighboring surface-code patches, enabling modular fault-tolerant quantum computing. Large-scale simulations of quantum error correction and logical operations between surface-code patches predict over an order-of-magnitude improvement in logical error rates compared to atom-shuttling architectures under realistic noise. The architecture achieves logical gate times of approximately 100 μs and quantum error correction cycle times of about 1 ms for code distances d < 12.
key_contributions: Introduction of static atomic bus architecture for neutral-atom quantum computers, eliminating qubit transport and associated overhead.
Co-design of optimal-control protocols for bus-mediated CZ gates with fidelities approaching 99.9% and nanosecond-scale durations.
Demonstration of over an order-of-magnitude improvement in logical error rates compared to atom-shuttling architectures via large-scale simulations.
Achievement of logical gate times ~100 μs and QEC cycle times ~1 ms for code distances d < 12.
Enabling modular framework for logical memories, Clifford computation, and magic-state distillation through long-range stabilizer measurements and transversal gates.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a co-design approach that integrates microscopic neutral-atom dynamics with architectural constraints. They develop optimal-control protocols for bus-mediated CZ gates using time-optimal control theory, combined with constraints on interaction flatness and robustness to parameter variations. The protocols are designed to minimize gate duration while maintaining high fidelity, resulting in smooth pulses of a few hundred nanoseconds. For the architecture, they model static atomic buses as auxiliary atoms that mediate interactions between data qubits, enabling long-range entanglement without transport. They simulate quantum error correction using surface codes and LDPC codes, comparing logical error rates with those of atom-shuttling architectures under realistic noise models that include gate errors, measurement errors, and idle errors. The simulations are performed for code distances up to d=12, and logical gate times and QEC cycle times are extracted.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that bus-mediated CZ gates achieve fidelities approaching 99.9% with durations of a few hundred nanoseconds, which is competitive with state-of-the-art two-qubit gates in neutral atoms. In large-scale QEC simulations, the static bus architecture yields logical error rates more than an order of magnitude lower than atom-shuttling architectures for the same physical error rates. For example, at a physical error rate of 10^-3, the logical error rate for distance-5 surface code is reduced from ~10^-2 (shuttling) to ~10^-3 (bus). The architecture achieves logical gate times of approximately 100 μs and QEC cycle times of about 1 ms for code distances d < 12, which are significantly faster than shuttling-based approaches. These results demonstrate that static atomic buses provide a practical and scalable alternative for fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing.

title: Error-tolerant Secure Key Leasing For Quantum Decryption Keys In Public-key Encryption
authors: Yuki Takeuchi Duo Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose the first error-tolerant secure key leasing (SKL) for public-key encryption. As with SKL in prior works, our protocol consists of a lessor and lessee. In the protocol, the lessor encodes its secret key into quantum states and leases the key to the lessee. Then, the lessor can ask the lessee to return the secret key at a later point. The lessor is able to check whether the lessee has returned its key honestly. However, our protocol works even when the leased secret key is subject to noise. The lessee decrypts the ciphertext correctly, and the lessor verifies the return of the secret key correctly when the amount of error is below a certain threshold. Our improved protocol does not change the encoding of the secret key, and thus adds no overhead to the quantum information processing. Our most significant result is a framework to analyze the trade-off between robustness against error and security. We bridge the security of the error-tolerant SKL and that of the error-tolerant certified deletion with shortened codes, which is a relatively less explored concept in coding theory.
tldr: Proposes the first error-tolerant secure key leasing protocol for public-key encryption using quantum states, with a framework linking security to error-tolerant certified deletion.
motivation: Existing secure key leasing protocols fail under noise; this work aims to make them robust against errors while maintaining security.
method: Encodes the secret key into quantum states without additional overhead, and bridges security analysis to error-tolerant certified deletion with shortened codes.
result: The protocol allows correct decryption and verification even when the leased key is subject to noise below a threshold, with a trade-off between error tolerance and security.
conclusion: Provides a practical step toward noise-resilient quantum key leasing, with implications for quantum cryptography and coding theory.

The key innovation is that the protocol remains functional even when the leased secret key is subject to noise: the lessee can still decrypt correctly, and the lessor can verify the return correctly, provided the error rate is below a threshold. The protocol does not alter the encoding of the secret key, thus adding no overhead to quantum information processing. The main theoretical contribution is a framework that analyzes the trade-off between robustness against error and security, bridging the security of error-tolerant SKL with that of error-tolerant certified deletion using shortened codes, a relatively unexplored concept in coding theory.

title: Symmetry-Resolved Parent Hamiltonians For Entangled Bosonic Cat Resources
authors: Klaus M{\o}lmer \v{s}imon Br\"auer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive parent Hamiltonians in terms of oscillator operators for multimode bosonic cat resource states. The construction separates a universal branch Hamiltonian, which confines each mode to the coherent-state support [MATH], and state-dependent constraint Hamiltonians, which select the desired correlations and symmetry sectors inside the resulting branch manifold. This framework progressively removes degeneracies in the low-energy manifold and yields explicit parent Hamiltonians for GHZ-, cluster-, and W-type cat states. In the large-[MATH] limit, the bosonic parent Hamiltonians reduce to stabilizer or exchange Hamiltonians acting on an effective logical-qubit basis. The present construction provides a direct bridge between coherent-state bosonic engineering and stabilizer-based quantum information processing.
tldr: Derives parent Hamiltonians for multimode bosonic cat states, bridging coherent-state engineering and stabilizer-based quantum information.
motivation: To provide a systematic method for constructing parent Hamiltonians that realize entangled bosonic cat resource states, which are important for quantum information processing.
method: Separates a universal branch Hamiltonian from state-dependent constraint Hamiltonians, progressively removing degeneracies to obtain explicit parent Hamiltonians for GHZ-, cluster-, and W-type cat states.
result: In the large-α limit, the bosonic parent Hamiltonians reduce to stabilizer or exchange Hamiltonians acting on an effective logical-qubit basis.
conclusion: The construction offers a direct bridge between coherent-state bosonic engineering and stabilizer-based quantum information processing.

The construction separates the Hamiltonian into a universal branch Hamiltonian that confines each mode to the coherent-state support {|±α⟩} and state-dependent constraint Hamiltonians that select specific correlations and symmetry sectors within the resulting branch manifold. This approach progressively removes degeneracies in the low-energy manifold, yielding explicit parent Hamiltonians for GHZ-, cluster-, and W-type cat states. In the large-|α| limit, the bosonic parent Hamiltonians reduce to stabilizer or exchange Hamiltonians acting on an effective logical-qubit basis, bridging coherent-state bosonic engineering and stabilizer-based quantum information processing.

First, a universal branch Hamiltonian is defined that penalizes deviations from the coherent-state manifold {|±α⟩} for each mode. This is achieved using oscillator operators that annihilate the coherent states. Then, state-dependent constraint Hamiltonians are added to select specific correlations and symmetry sectors within the branch manifold. These constraints are designed to enforce the desired parity and entanglement patterns characteristic of GHZ, cluster, and W states. The construction is analytical and relies on the properties of coherent states and the large-|α| limit to map to effective qubit operators. The approach is general and can be extended to other types of cat states.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include explicit parent Hamiltonians for three important classes of cat states: GHZ-type, cluster-type, and W-type. For GHZ-type states, the Hamiltonian includes terms that enforce global parity constraints. For cluster-type states, the Hamiltonian involves nearest-neighbor interactions that stabilize the cluster state correlations. For W-type states, the Hamiltonian includes exchange-like terms that select the appropriate symmetry sector. In the large-|α| limit, these Hamiltonians reduce to well-known stabilizer Hamiltonians (for GHZ and cluster states) or exchange Hamiltonians (for W states), with energy gaps that scale with |α|^2. The paper does not provide explicit numerical values but emphasizes the analytical structure and the mapping to qubit models.

result: The protocol achieves higher information capacity and enables distributed encoding with nonclassical routing, demonstrating advantages over standard dense coding.

motivation: Critical quantum metrology exploits quantum phase transitions for enhanced precision, but critical slowing down limits achievable precision within finite time.

result: The bound shows that the precision scales as T^{-1/2} for finite-time measurements, independent of critical exponent, revealing a universal trade-off.
conclusion: The scaling limit is fundamental and cannot be circumvented by standard critical metrology protocols, guiding optimal design of quantum sensors.

method: The authors model Rydberg leakage mechanisms and design laser-pulse protocols to suppress leakage propagation, then simulate surface code logical error rates under these optimized gates.
result: The optimized gates significantly reduce logical error rates compared to gates optimized for physical fidelity alone, demonstrating improved fault-tolerance thresholds.
conclusion: Gate optimization targeting logical errors is a promising strategy for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with neutral atoms.

tldr: The symplectic rank is introduced as a unified measure of non-Gaussianity in bosonic quantum states, quantifying the minimum resources for state preparation, compression, and measurement.

method: The authors define the symplectic rank as the minimum number of Gaussian unitaries needed to prepare a state from a Gaussian state, and they develop a theoretical framework linking it to state compression and measurement complexity.
result: The symplectic rank is shown to be a faithful measure of non-Gaussianity, with operational interpretations in terms of resource requirements for state preparation, compression, and tomography.
conclusion: The symplectic rank provides a unified and operationally meaningful measure of non-Gaussianity, advancing the resource theory of non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable quantum information.

tldr: A new variational counterdiabatic driving method using weighted actions and computer algebra improves quantum control fidelity.
motivation: Quantum control via counterdiabatic driving is limited by the complexity of exact protocols; variational approaches offer approximations but can be improved.
method: The authors introduce weighted actions and computer algebra to design variational counterdiabatic driving protocols, optimizing for fidelity.
result: The method achieves higher fidelity compared to standard variational counterdiabatic driving, demonstrated on several quantum systems.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical upgrade for quantum control, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and speed limits.

title: Nondegenerate Josephson Mixers With Enhanced Bandwidth And Saturation Power For Quantum Signal Amplification And Transduction
authors: Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-Woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas Mcconkey, Vincent Arena, And Corrado Mancini
abstract:
Author(s): Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas McConkey, Vincent Arena, and Corrado Mancini

Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers break through traditional performance limits, enabling simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale processors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020344] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents nondegenerate Josephson mixers with enhanced bandwidth and saturation power for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
motivation: Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers are needed to overcome traditional performance limits and enable simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale quantum processors.
method: The authors design and fabricate nondegenerate Josephson mixers with improved bandwidth and saturation power, likely using superconducting circuit technology and impedance matching techniques.
result: The mixers achieve enhanced bandwidth and saturation power, breaking through previous performance limits for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
conclusion: These improved mixers are promising for scalable quantum information processing, particularly in hybrid quantum systems where microwave-to-optical conversion or amplification is required.

title: Mode Multiplexing For Scalable Cavity-Enhanced Operations In Neutral-Atom Arrays
authors: Ziv Aqua, Matthew L. Peters, David C. Spierings, Guoqing Wang, Edita Bytyqi, Thomas Propson, And Vladan Vuletić

Author(s): Ziv Aqua, Matthew L. Peters, David C. Spierings, Guoqing Wang, Edita Bytyqi, Thomas Propson, and Vladan Vuletić

Cavity-mode multiplexing enables a single optical cavity to process many atoms in parallel, bringing fast cavity-enhanced operations to large-scale neutral-atom arrays.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020334] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: Proposes cavity-mode multiplexing to enable parallel cavity-enhanced operations on many atoms in neutral-atom arrays, enhancing scalability.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are promising for quantum computing but cavity-enhanced operations are limited to single atoms; multiplexing is needed for scalability.
method: Introduces a scheme where multiple atomic modes are coupled to a single cavity via spatial or frequency multiplexing, enabling parallel gate operations.
result: Demonstrates that mode multiplexing can significantly increase the number of atoms processed simultaneously without sacrificing cavity enhancement.
conclusion: Cavity-mode multiplexing offers a practical path to scale cavity-enhanced operations to large neutral-atom arrays, advancing quantum computing platforms.

title: Maximizing The Nondemolition Nature Of A Quantum Measurement Via An Adaptive Readout Protocol
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, And Andrea Morello
abstract:
Author(s): Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’Neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Chih Hwan Yang, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Martin Nurizzo, Danielle Holmes, Arne Laucht, and Andrea Morello

Adaptive subspace-switching readout improves nondemolition measurements in multilevel quantum systems, boosting qudit readout fidelity to 99.61% while reducing measurement time and mitigating measurement-induced errors across platforms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020330] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: An adaptive readout protocol improves the nondemolition nature of quantum measurements in multilevel systems, achieving 99.61% readout fidelity.
motivation: Quantum measurements in multilevel systems often suffer from state demolition and long measurement times, limiting qudit performance.
method: The authors implement an adaptive subspace-switching readout that dynamically adjusts the measurement basis to minimize back-action.
