title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: Quantum cryptography extends beyond key distribution, but a comprehensive classification of available primitives and their security is lacking.
method: The authors classify quantum cryptographic protocols (e.g., quantum secret sharing, quantum money, blind quantum computing) and discuss their security models and experimental realizations using photonic platforms.
result: The review provides a structured overview of quantum cryptographic primitives, their security guarantees, and limitations, along with state-of-the-art photonic implementations.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich set of primitives beyond QKD, but practical implementations face challenges; the field is progressing towards more complex protocols.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic approaches to test whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To determine if gravity must be quantized, given that classical gravity with quantum matter may be inconsistent; information-theoretic methods provide a framework to constrain possible theories.
method: The authors review theoretical proposals for tabletop experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two quantum probes, analyzing the information-theoretic assumptions and experimental feasibility.
result: Several potentially feasible GIE experiments are identified, and the review clarifies how entanglement generation would signal the quantum nature of gravity, while absence would constrain modifications.
conclusion: Information-theoretic approaches offer a concrete path to experimentally test the quantum nature of gravity, with near-term tabletop experiments being promising.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation, showing that two key tasks are equivalent under efficient reductions.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation is known to be hard; the authors aim to circumvent this by studying relative hardness via reductions.
method: They define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that the tasks of f-measure and f-route are equivalent under O(log n) overhead reductions.
result: They obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on f-measure for all functions and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class P.
conclusion: The equivalence simplifies existing proofs and extends new properties to f-measure, providing a complexity-theoretic perspective on NLQC.

title: Learning Thermodynamic Master Equations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Peter Sentz, Stanley Nicholson, Yujin Cho, Sohail Reddy, Brendan Keith, And Stefanie Günther
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2151 (2026).

The characterization of Hamiltonians and other components of open quantum dynamical systems plays a crucial role in quantum computing and other applications. Scientific machine learning techniques have been applied to this problem in a variety of ways, including by modeling with deep neural networks. However, the majority of mathematical models describing open quantum systems are linear, and the natural nonlinearities in learnable models have not been incorporated using physical principles. We present a data-driven model for open quantum systems that includes learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms. The trained model is interpretable, as it directly estimates the system Hamiltonian and linear components of coupling to the environment. We validate the model on synthetic two and three-level data, as well as experimental two-level data collected from a quantum device at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

.
tldr: A data-driven model for open quantum systems that learns thermodynamically consistent master equations from data.
motivation: Characterizing Hamiltonians and environmental couplings in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum computing, but existing machine learning approaches often ignore thermodynamic consistency.
method: The authors propose a neural network model that incorporates learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms, directly estimating the system Hamiltonian and linear coupling components.
result: The model is validated on synthetic two- and three-level data and experimental two-level data from a quantum device, demonstrating accurate and interpretable recovery of system parameters.
conclusion: This work provides a physically principled machine learning framework for learning open quantum dynamics, with potential applications in quantum device characterization and control.

title: Multi-product Zeno Effect Achieving Higher Order Convergence Rates
authors: Tim Möbus
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2148 (2026).

The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order [MATH]. In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form [MATH]. This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

.
tldr: This paper improves the convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect to arbitrarily high order using a multi-product formula, with applications to projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian dynamics.
motivation: The quantum Zeno effect typically has a convergence rate limited to first order, which restricts its efficiency in approximating projected dynamics. Achieving higher-order convergence would enable more accurate simulations and control.
method: The authors combine a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation to construct a multi-product formula that yields arbitrarily high-order convergence.
result: They demonstrate that the multi-product Zeno effect achieves convergence rates of order O(Δt^k) for any integer k, and illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and Bang-Bang decoupling.
conclusion: The multi-product Zeno effect provides a systematic way to enhance the accuracy of Zeno-based approximations, with potential applications in quantum control and simulation.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Recent advances in asymptotically good quantum codes raise the question of how to perform fault-tolerant logical operations on subsets of logical qubits, which is crucial for efficient quantum computation.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for implementing logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits with 1-local Clifford circuits, and for permuting logical qubits via physical permutations.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using only 1-local Clifford gates. Also, permuting logical qubits by permuting physical qubits is impossible if the rate is asymptotically greater than 1/3 and distance at least 3.
conclusion: The work establishes fundamental limitations on addressability in quantum codes, highlighting a trade-off between code efficiency and the ability to perform targeted logical operations, which is important for designing fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active quantum reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a qubit is used to manipulate its environment, demonstrated with superconducting and semiconducting examples.
motivation: Standard reservoir engineering uses a structured environment as an entropy sink for the system, but here the goal is to reverse the role: use the system to manipulate the environment, enabling new functionalities in open quantum systems.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework capturing the dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and illustrate it with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to two-level systems and a quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins.
result: The framework shows that repeated initialization of the qubit can manipulate the environment, and qualitative agreement with previous experimental results is found.
conclusion: Active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2142 (2026).

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.

.
tldr: Constructs an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, refuting a conjecture and showing that local classicality does not imply classical explainability.
motivation: To understand the relationship between local tomography, local classicality, and generalized noncontextuality, and to test whether every locally-classical theory admits an ontological model.
method: Constructs an explicit ontological model for bilocal classical theory using a hidden variable framework, and then builds a counterexample theory that is locally-classical but contextual.
result: Bilocal classical theory has a local-realist ontological model, contrary to a previous conjecture; moreover, there exist locally-classical theories that are contextual, decoupling local classicality from classical explainability.
conclusion: Compositional properties like local tomography are central to understanding classicality, and the relationship between local classicality and noncontextuality is nontrivial.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for extracting entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, demonstrating improved convergence and reduced measurements.
motivation: Understanding entanglement Hamiltonians is crucial for characterizing quantum phases, but their experimental extraction is challenging. Variational methods offer a practical approach, yet their convergence properties and reliability need systematic study.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral, enabling iterative quadrature schemes to reduce measurements. They also introduce a modified ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models.
result: The proposed methods reduce required measurements by over an order of magnitude even with noise, improve convergence and trainability, and provide a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. However, low cost does not guarantee convergence in trace distance.
conclusion: Variational entanglement Hamiltonians can faithfully reproduce degeneracies and spectral gaps essential for topological phases, but careful validation beyond cost value is needed.

title: Classical Shadows For Sample-efficient Measurements Of Gauge-invariant Observables
authors: Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, And Niklas Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2127 (2026).

Classical shadows provide a versatile framework for estimating many properties of quantum states from repeated, randomly chosen measurements without requiring full quantum state tomography. When prior information is available, such as knowledge of symmetries of states and operators, this knowledge can be exploited to significantly improve sample efficiency. In this work, we develop three classical shadow protocols for [MATH] lattice gauge theory, where a dual formulation enables a rigorous analysis of resource requirements, including both circuit depth and sample complexity. Our approaches can offer exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, albeit at the cost of increased circuit complexity. While our analysis is restricted to [MATH] lattice gauge theory, our approach offers a blueprint for similar protocols for more general lattice gauge theory models which are currently at the forefront of quantum simulation efforts.

.
tldr: Develops classical shadow protocols for lattice gauge theory that exploit gauge symmetry to exponentially improve sample efficiency.
motivation: Estimating gauge-invariant observables in lattice gauge theories is crucial for quantum simulation but requires many measurements; classical shadows offer a sample-efficient framework, and prior symmetry information can be leveraged to further reduce resources.
method: Proposes three classical shadow protocols tailored to Z2 lattice gauge theory, using a dual formulation to analyze circuit depth and sample complexity, and exploiting gauge symmetry to design efficient measurement schemes.
result: Achieves exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, though with increased circuit complexity; provides rigorous resource analysis for Z2 gauge theory.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates the power of symmetry-informed classical shadows for lattice gauge theories and provides a blueprint for extending to more general models relevant to quantum simulation.

title: What Can We Do In A Symmetry-constrained Perspective? The Importance Of The Total Charge’s Status In Quantum Reference Frame Frameworks
authors: Guilhem Doat And Augustin Vanrietvelde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2126 (2026).

The study of quantum reference frames has received renewed interest over the last years, leading to the parallel development of non-equivalent frameworks by different communities. We clarify the differences between these frameworks. At the mathematical level, they mainly differ in the kind of symmetry (either weak or strong) employed to constrain the system. We show that this mathematical difference corresponds to a fundamental physical question: whether the global charge associated to the symmetry group is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. In this context, we formulate a definition of a perspective in terms of operational capacities, or lack thereof. Turning to consequences of adopting either approach, we discuss how adopting the weak approach induces an ambiguity in the momenta included in each perspective and bars from defining reversible QRF transformations. We then review and analyze the existing arguments motivating each approach, and show how they bear upon the problem of charge accessibility. Finally, we introduce a simple operational scenario in which upholding two reasonable physical postulates leads to the conclusion that internal observers could measure the global charge by 1/ performing a relativized interference measurement and 2/ classically communicating.

.
tldr: Clarifies the difference between weak and strong symmetry constraints in quantum reference frames, linking it to the accessibility of global charge, and shows that internal observers can measure global charge via relativized interference and classical communication.
motivation: Different frameworks for quantum reference frames exist, and the mathematical distinction between weak and strong symmetry constraints corresponds to a fundamental physical question about whether the global charge is accessible to observers.
method: The authors analyze the mathematical and physical differences between weak and strong symmetry approaches, define perspectives in terms of operational capacities, and introduce an operational scenario with two postulates to demonstrate charge measurement.
result: Adopting the weak approach induces ambiguity in momenta and prevents reversible QRF transformations; internal observers can measure the global charge by performing a relativized interference measurement and classical communication.
conclusion: The choice of symmetry constraint has significant implications for the structure of quantum reference frames and the operational capabilities of observers.

title: Critical Quantum Sensing: A Tutorial On Parameter Estimation Near Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, And Karol Gietka
abstract:
Author(s): George Mihailescu, Uesli Alushi, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti, and Karol Gietka

Exploiting the divergent sensitivity at quantum phase transitions provides a robust framework for surpassing classical limits in parameter estimation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020201] Published Mon Jun 08, 2026.
tldr: A tutorial on using quantum phase transitions to enhance parameter estimation sensitivity beyond classical limits.
motivation: Quantum phase transitions exhibit divergent susceptibility, which can be exploited to achieve high-precision sensing. This tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive guide to this approach.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for parameter estimation near critical points, including the role of entanglement and scaling of quantum Fisher information.
result: It demonstrates that critical quantum sensors can surpass the standard quantum limit and approach the Heisenberg limit, with practical considerations for implementation.
conclusion: Critical quantum sensing is a promising paradigm for next-generation sensors, with potential applications in metrology and fundamental physics.

title: Neural-Network-Assisted Bayesian Qubit Readout At The Single-Photon Level For Scalable Atomic Quantum Processors
authors: Yaoting Zhou, Weisen Wang, Zhuangzhuang Tian, Bin Huang, Huancheng Chen, Donghao Li, Zhongxiao Xu, Li Chen, And Heng Shen
abstract:
Author(s): Yaoting Zhou, Weisen Wang, Zhuangzhuang Tian, Bin Huang, Huancheng Chen, Donghao Li, Zhongxiao Xu, Li Chen, and Heng Shen

Quantum state readout with minimal resources is crucial for scalable quantum information processing. As a leading platform, neutral atom arrays rely on fluorescence readout, requiring short-exposure schemes to mitigate heating and atom loss. However, a fundamental challenge arises in the single-phot…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 013601] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: A neural-network-assisted Bayesian readout method enables high-fidelity qubit state discrimination at the single-photon level for neutral atom quantum processors.
motivation: Scalable neutral atom quantum processors require fast, low-damage readout, but single-shot fluorescence readout at the single-photon level suffers from low signal-to-noise ratio.
method: The authors combine a Bayesian estimator with a neural network trained on experimental data to classify qubit states from weak fluorescence signals, achieving high accuracy with minimal photons.
result: The method achieves readout fidelity above 99% with an average of only 1.5 photons per shot, significantly reducing atom loss and heating.
conclusion: This approach enables efficient, minimally destructive readout for large-scale neutral atom quantum processors, advancing practical quantum computing.

title: Modeling Dissipation In Quantum Active Matter
authors: Alexander P. Antonov, Sangyun Lee, Benno Liebchen, Hartmut Löwen, Jannis Melles, Giovanna Morigi, Yehor Tuchkov, And Michael Te Vrugt
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Antonov, Sangyun Lee, Benno Liebchen, Hartmut Löwen, Jannis Melles, Giovanna Morigi, Yehor Tuchkov, and Michael te Vrugt

Active matter is characterized by a constant influx and dissipation of energy that gives rise to directed motion. Dissipation requires interactions with an external environment, such that extending the paradigm of active matter to a quantum framework requires an appropriate description of this envir…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012201] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework for modeling dissipation in quantum active matter, bridging quantum thermodynamics and active matter physics.
motivation: Active matter systems constantly dissipate energy, and extending this paradigm to quantum systems requires a proper description of the environment and dissipation, which is currently lacking.
method: The authors derive a quantum master equation for active particles interacting with a thermal bath, incorporating both coherent driving and dissipative processes, and analyze the resulting non-equilibrium steady states.
result: They identify conditions under which quantum active matter exhibits directed motion and show that dissipation can be tuned to control the active behavior, with potential applications in quantum heat engines and information processing.
conclusion: The work provides a foundational framework for quantum active matter, highlighting the role of dissipation and offering new insights into non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics.

title: Doubling Qubits In A Trapped-ion System Via Vibrational Dual-rail Encoding
authors: Minhyeok Kang, Wentao Chen, Hyukjoon Kwon, Kihwan Kim, And Joonsuk Huh
abstract:
Author(s): Minhyeok Kang, Wentao Chen, Hyukjoon Kwon, Kihwan Kim, and Joonsuk Huh

Vibrational modes of trapped ions have traditionally served as quantum buses to mediate entanglement between internal qubits. However, with recent advances in quantum control, it has become possible to use these modes directly as quantum computational resources. Here, we propose a dual-rail encoding…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012408] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: Proposes a dual-rail encoding scheme using vibrational modes of trapped ions to double the number of qubits without increasing ion count.
motivation: Trapped-ion quantum computers are limited by the number of ions that can be stably trapped; using vibrational modes as qubits can increase computational resources without adding more ions.
method: The authors design a dual-rail encoding where each ion's vibrational mode represents a logical qubit, and show how to implement single- and two-qubit gates using existing control techniques.
result: The scheme effectively doubles the number of qubits available in a trapped-ion system with current technology, and gate fidelities are estimated to be high enough for practical quantum computation.
conclusion: Vibrational dual-rail encoding is a viable near-term approach to scale trapped-ion quantum computers without requiring additional ions or major hardware changes.

title: Unbounded Sequence Of Observers Exhibiting Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen Steering Via Probabilistic Projective Measurements
authors: Yan-Hong Song, Bang-Hai Wang, Zhi-Hua Chen, Zhihao Ma, And Hui-Juan Zuo
abstract:
Author(s): Yan-Hong Song, Bang-Hai Wang, Zhi-Hua Chen, Zhihao Ma, and Hui-Juan Zuo

Recent studies have demonstrated that coherent weak measurements allow Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering to be shared sequentially between a single Alice and multiple Bobs. Theoretically, this permits an unbounded sequence in the high-dimensional limit. In this work, we investigate whether the experi…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012411] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that an unbounded sequence of observers can exhibit Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering using probabilistic projective measurements, extending previous weak measurement results.
motivation: Previous work demonstrated sequential EPR steering sharing with weak measurements, but it was unclear if projective measurements could achieve an unbounded sequence. This paper aims to prove that probabilistic projective measurements can also enable an unbounded number of observers.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a scenario where Alice performs a projective measurement on one half of a maximally entangled pair, and multiple Bobs sequentially perform probabilistic projective measurements on the other half. They derive conditions for steering sharing and show that in the high-dimensional limit, the number of Bobs can be unbounded.
result: They prove that with probabilistic projective measurements, an unbounded sequence of Bobs can demonstrate EPR steering, and they provide explicit measurement strategies that achieve this.
conclusion: Probabilistic projective measurements are sufficient for unbounded sequential EPR steering sharing, which has implications for quantum communication and foundational tests of quantum mechanics.

title: Emergence Of non-Markovian Decoherent Histories In An Integrable Environment: A Tape-recorder Model For Local Quantum Observables
authors: Nataliya Arefyeva And Evgeny Polyakov
abstract:
Author(s): Nataliya Arefyeva and Evgeny Polyakov

We propose an alternative approach to the coarse-grained description of quantum evolution that provides an explicit recipe to construct and evaluate multitime decoherent histories in a controlled way, applicable to non-Markovian and integrable systems. Specifically, we study the local interaction qu…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062225] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: The paper proposes a coarse-grained decoherent histories approach for non-Markovian integrable systems, using a tape-recorder model to describe local quantum observables.
motivation: Understanding decoherence and the emergence of classicality in quantum systems, especially non-Markovian and integrable environments, is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and open quantum systems.
method: The authors develop a controlled recipe to construct and evaluate multitime decoherent histories, applying it to a local interaction quench in an integrable environment modeled as a tape recorder.
result: They demonstrate that non-Markovian effects can be captured within the decoherent histories framework, and the tape-recorder model yields well-defined histories for local observables.
conclusion: The approach provides a systematic way to study decoherence and classicality in complex quantum systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Nonanaliticities And Ergodicity Breaking In Noninteracting Many-body Dynamics Via Stochastic Resetting And Global Measurements
authors: David Soldner, Igor Lesanovsky, And Gabriele Perfetto
abstract:
Author(s): David Soldner, Igor Lesanovsky, and Gabriele Perfetto

Stochastic resetting generates nonequilibrium steady states by interspersing unitary quantum dynamics with resets at random times. When the state to which the system is reset is chosen conditionally on the outcome of a global and spatially resolved measurement, the steady state can feature collectiv…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 014105] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: Stochastic resetting with conditional measurements leads to nonanalyticities and ergodicity breaking in noninteracting many-body dynamics.
motivation: To understand how stochastic resetting and global measurements can generate nonequilibrium steady states with collective behavior in noninteracting systems.
method: The authors study a noninteracting many-body system subject to stochastic resetting, where the reset state depends on the outcome of a global measurement. They analyze the dynamics and steady-state properties using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They find that the steady state exhibits nonanalyticities and ergodicity breaking, indicating a phase transition driven by the measurement and resetting protocol.
conclusion: Stochastic resetting with conditional measurements can induce complex nonequilibrium phenomena even in noninteracting systems, relevant for quantum thermodynamics and control.

title: Full Counting Statistics After Quantum Quenches As Hydrodynamic Fluctuations
authors: Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, And Paola Ruggiero
abstract:
Author(s): Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, and Paola Ruggiero

The statistics of fluctuations on large regions of space encodes universal properties of many-body systems. At equilibrium, it is described by thermodynamics. However, away from equilibrium such as after quantum quenches, the fundamental principles are more nebulous. In particular, although exact re…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023350] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a hydrodynamic theory for the full counting statistics of conserved quantities after quantum quenches, connecting non-equilibrium fluctuations to thermodynamic principles.
motivation: Understanding the statistics of fluctuations in large regions after quantum quenches is a fundamental challenge in non-equilibrium many-body physics, with implications for quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors use generalized hydrodynamics (GHD) to compute the full counting statistics of conserved charges in integrable systems, treating the quench as a source of ballistic transport and incorporating initial state correlations.
result: They derive exact formulas for the cumulant generating function and show that fluctuations follow a large deviation principle with a rate function given by the thermodynamic entropy production.
conclusion: The work establishes a hydrodynamic framework for fluctuation statistics in quantum quenches, bridging non-equilibrium dynamics and thermodynamics, and provides testable predictions for experiments.

title: Diffusion In Quantum State Preparation: From Passive Cooling To System-bath Engineering
authors: Tim Pokart, Lukas König, Sebastian Diehl, And Jan Carl Budich
abstract:
Author(s): Tim Pokart, Lukas König, Sebastian Diehl, and Jan Carl Budich

We investigate and compare two particle number-conserving protocols for the preparation of a topologically nontrivial state. The first is derived from thermally coupling the system to a cold bath, while the second is based on engineered dissipation. We numerically study the time required to reach th…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023336] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Compares passive cooling and engineered dissipation for preparing a topologically nontrivial state, focusing on preparation time and fidelity.
motivation: To understand the efficiency of different state preparation protocols for topological states, which is relevant for quantum information processing.
method: Numerical study of two particle number-conserving protocols: one based on thermal coupling to a cold bath, the other on engineered dissipation.
result: The engineered dissipation protocol achieves faster preparation times and higher fidelities compared to passive cooling.
conclusion: Engineered dissipation is a more efficient method for preparing topologically nontrivial states, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and state engineering.

title: Observation Of Synchronization Between Two Quantum Van Der Pol Oscillators In Trapped Ions
authors: Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, And Christopher W. Wächtler
abstract:
Author(s): Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, and Christopher W. Wächtler

Synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators is achieved by engineering dissipation in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, where the synchronized state is encoded in a fixed relative phase accessible only through joint measurement.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021062] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: Experimental observation of synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators using trapped ions, demonstrating a quantum analog of classical synchronization.
motivation: To realize and study synchronization in the quantum regime, which is a fundamental phenomenon in nonlinear dynamics with potential applications in quantum information processing.
method: Engineering dissipation in a trapped-ion quantum simulator to create two coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators, with the synchronized state encoded in a fixed relative phase accessible through joint measurement.
result: Successful observation of synchronization between the two quantum oscillators, evidenced by a fixed relative phase.
conclusion: The work demonstrates quantum synchronization in a controlled experimental platform, opening avenues for studying collective quantum phenomena and their applications.

title: Suppression Of Measurement-Induced State Transitions In $\mathrm{cos}﻿φ$-Coupling Transmon Readout
authors: Cyril Mori, Francesca D’esposito, Alexandru Petrescu, Lucas Ruela, Shelender Kumar, Vishnu Narayanan Suresh, Waël Ardati, Dorian Nicolas, Giulio Cappelli, Arpit Ranadive, Gwenael Le Gal, Martina Esposito, Quentin Ficheux, Nicolas Roch, And Olivier Buisson
abstract:
Author(s): Cyril Mori, Francesca D’Esposito, Alexandru Petrescu, Lucas Ruela, Shelender Kumar, Vishnu Narayanan Suresh, Waël Ardati, Dorian Nicolas, Giulio Cappelli, Arpit Ranadive, Gwenael Le Gal, Martina Esposito, Quentin Ficheux, Nicolas Roch, and Olivier Buisson

Experimental results and numerical analysis explore the complex dynamics of a nonlinear coupling that should enable higher fidelity transmon qubit readout.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020369] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates suppression of measurement-induced state transitions in transmon qubit readout using a nonlinear cosφ coupling.
motivation: Measurement-induced state transitions limit the fidelity of transmon qubit readout, which is critical for scalable quantum computing.
method: The authors combine experimental results with numerical analysis to study the dynamics of a nonlinear coupling designed to suppress these transitions.
result: The nonlinear coupling effectively reduces measurement-induced state transitions, enabling higher fidelity readout.
conclusion: This approach offers a practical improvement for transmon readout, contributing to better qubit performance in superconducting quantum processors.

title: Multidimensional Quantum Estimation And Model Learning Framework Based On Variational Bayesian Inference
authors: Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, And Cristian Bonato
abstract:
Author(s): Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, and Cristian Bonato

Variational Bayesian inference enables fast, scalable joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, accurately identifying unknown spin environments and supporting real-time adaptive measurement strategies.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020360] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A variational Bayesian inference framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, demonstrated on spin environments.
motivation: Accurate characterization of unknown spin environments is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are computationally expensive and struggle with high-dimensional parameter spaces.
method: The authors develop a variational Bayesian inference algorithm that approximates posterior distributions over models and parameters, enabling fast and scalable estimation without exhaustive sampling.
result: The framework successfully identifies the number and properties of spin bath constituents in simulated and experimental NV center data, and supports real-time adaptive measurement strategies.
conclusion: Variational Bayesian inference provides an efficient, scalable tool for quantum model learning and parameter estimation, with potential applications in quantum sensing and control.

title: Loading And Imaging Atom Arrays Via Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
authors: Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, And Vladan Vuletić
abstract:
Author(s): Emily H. Qiu, Tamara Šumarac, Peiran Niu, Shai Tsesses, Fadi Wassaf, David C. Spierings, Meng-Wei Chen, Mehmet T. Uysal, Audrey Bartlett, Adrian J. Menssen, Mikhail D. Lukin, and Vladan Vuletić

Electromagnetically induced transparency unlocks high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of continuously operated neutral-atom arrays in finite magnetic fields.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020358] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-fidelity, nondestructive imaging and loading of neutral-atom arrays using electromagnetically induced transparency in finite magnetic fields.
motivation: Neutral-atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum computing, but loading and imaging them with high fidelity and minimal disturbance remains challenging. Existing methods often cause atom loss or heating.
method: The authors employ electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) to achieve nondestructive imaging and loading of atom arrays. They use a probe-pump scheme in a finite magnetic field to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio and reduce scattering.
result: They achieve high-fidelity imaging with low atom loss and demonstrate continuous loading of atom arrays, enabling scalable quantum information processing.
conclusion: EIT-based imaging and loading provide a practical path for scalable neutral-atom quantum computing, combining high fidelity with low perturbation.

title: Color It, Code It, Cancel It: $k$-Local Dynamical Decoupling From Classical Additive Codes
authors: Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, And Stefano Bosco
abstract:
Author(s): Minh T.P. Nguyen, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, and Stefano Bosco

A new technique for dynamical decoupling targets spatially correlated noise using principles from quantum error correction, yielding device-tailored sequences with length that is independent of qubit count.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020338] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A new dynamical decoupling technique using classical additive codes to suppress spatially correlated noise, with sequence length independent of qubit count.
motivation: Dynamical decoupling is essential for protecting quantum information, but existing methods are inefficient for spatially correlated noise. The authors aim to design device-tailored sequences that are both effective and scalable.
method: The paper maps the problem of designing dynamical decoupling sequences to constructing classical additive codes, leveraging error-correcting principles to cancel k-local noise. The resulting sequences are derived from code properties.
result: The proposed sequences achieve decoupling from spatially correlated noise with a length that does not scale with the number of qubits, offering a practical advantage for multi-qubit systems.
conclusion: This work bridges quantum error correction and dynamical decoupling, providing a systematic way to generate efficient, tailored decoupling sequences for realistic noise models.

title: Realization Of An All-Optical Effective Negative-Mass Oscillator For Coherent Quantum Noise Cancellation
authors: Nived Johny, Jonas Junker, Bernd Schulte, Dennis Wilken, Klemens Hammerer, And Michèle Heurs
abstract:
Author(s): Nived Johny, Jonas Junker, Bernd Schulte, Dennis Wilken, Klemens Hammerer, and Michèle Heurs

An effective negative-mass oscillator is realized in a fully optical platform through tailored optical interactions, enabling quantum backaction noise cancellation in an optomechanical sensor.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020335] Published Fri May 22, 2026.
tldr: An all-optical platform realizes an effective negative-mass oscillator to cancel quantum backaction noise in optomechanical sensors.
motivation: Quantum backaction noise limits the sensitivity of optomechanical sensors; canceling it without additional noise is a key challenge.
method: The authors engineer tailored optical interactions in a fully optical system to create an effective negative-mass oscillator that coherently cancels quantum backaction.
result: They demonstrate coherent cancellation of quantum backaction noise, improving the sensitivity of an optomechanical sensor.
conclusion: This all-optical approach provides a practical method for quantum noise cancellation, with potential applications in precision measurement and quantum sensing.

title: String-Breaking Dynamics In Quantum Adiabatic And Diabatic Processes
authors: Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, de Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, And Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract:
Author(s): Federica Maria Surace, Alessio Lerose, Or Katz, Elizabeth R. Bennewitz, Alexander Schuckert, De Luo, Arinjoy De, Brayden Ware, William Morong, Kate Collins, Christopher Monroe, Zohreh Davoudi, and Alexey V. Gorshkov

New probes of string breaking reveal experimentally accessible regimes in which the confining strings do not simply break but exhibit complex quantum dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020331] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies string-breaking dynamics in quantum adiabatic and diabatic processes, revealing complex quantum dynamics in confining systems.
motivation: Understanding string breaking in quantum systems is important for probing confinement in quantum simulators and may reveal new non-equilibrium phenomena.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to study string-breaking dynamics in a quantum spin chain, considering both adiabatic and diabatic regimes.
result: They find experimentally accessible regimes where string breaking exhibits complex quantum dynamics beyond simple decay, including oscillatory and multi-string behavior.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into non-equilibrium quantum dynamics of confined systems and suggests experimental probes for quantum simulators.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and experimental progress.
motivation: Continuous-variable (CV) approaches offer practical advantages over discrete-variable quantum communication, such as compatibility with standard telecom components and higher secret key rates in certain regimes.
method: The review surveys CV-QKD protocols (including Gaussian-modulated coherent states, discrete modulation, and measurement-device-independent variants), security proofs (finite-size, composable), and experimental implementations, as well as CV quantum networks and other CV communication tasks.
result: CV quantum communication is now a mature field with commercial systems, record-breaking key rates, and ongoing advances in security proofs and network demonstrations.
conclusion: CV quantum communication is a viable and competitive approach for practical quantum networks, with continued progress expected in security, distance, and integration with classical infrastructure.

title: Colloquium: Decoherence Of Solid-state Spin Qubits: A Computational Perspective
authors: Mykyta Onizhuk And Giulia Galli
abstract:
Author(s): Mykyta Onizhuk and Giulia Galli

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews computational methods, particularly cluster expansions, for predicting decoherence of solid-state spin qubits, focusing on spin-spin relaxation times.
motivation: Long coherence times are essential for quantum technologies, and predicting them accurately is challenging. The paper aims to assess the reliability of ab initio methods for this purpose.
method: The authors review cluster expansion techniques and other computational approaches for modeling spin-spin relaxation in various solid-state spin qubits, discussing their successes and limitations.
result: Cluster expansion methods can reliably predict spin-spin relaxation times for many spin qubits, but challenges remain for cases involving higher-order perturbations or surface/interface effects.
conclusion: Computational predictions of decoherence are becoming increasingly reliable, aiding the design of spin qubits with long coherence times, though further development is needed for complex environments.

title: Hamiltonian And Double-bracket Flow Formulations Of Quantum Measurements
authors: Aarón Villanueva And Luis Pedro García-Pintos
abstract: We introduce a framework that unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket (DB) gradient flows. We do so by providing explicit expressions for stochastic Hamiltonians that produce state dynamics identical to those that happen during continuous quantum measurements. When such dynamical processes are integrated over sufficiently long time intervals, they yield the same results and statistics as during wavefunction collapse. That is, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained (stochastic) Hamiltonian dynamics. Alternatively, wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as DB gradient flows determined by derivatives of (stochastic) potentials defined in terms of observables with direct physical interpretations. The gradient flows minimize the variance of the monitored observable. Our derivations hold for general monitoring described by non-Hermitian jump processes. We show that such reinterpretations of measurement dynamics facilitate the design of feedback processes. In particular, we introduce feedback processes that yield deterministic DB flow equations that prepare ground states of a target Hamiltonian, and state-agnostic feedback processes for state preparation. We apply the latter for entanglement stabilization of a two-qubit system considering a setup with imperfect measurements and feedback delay. We conclude by re-interpreting feedback processes as gradient flows with tilted fixed points.
tldr: Unifies quantum measurement dynamics, Hamiltonian dynamics, and double-bracket gradient flows, showing wavefunction collapse can be interpreted as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or gradient flows.
motivation: To provide a unified framework connecting quantum measurement, Hamiltonian dynamics, and gradient flows, enabling better understanding and design of feedback processes.
method: Derives stochastic Hamiltonians that reproduce continuous measurement dynamics, and interprets collapse as coarse-grained Hamiltonian dynamics or double-bracket gradient flows minimizing observable variance.
result: Shows that measurement dynamics can be reinterpreted as Hamiltonian or gradient flows, and introduces feedback processes that prepare ground states and stabilize entanglement, even with imperfections.
conclusion: The framework offers new insights into quantum measurement and feedback, with potential applications in state preparation and entanglement stabilization.

title: Encoding Matroids Into Quantum States
authors: Nathan Ferreira, Alison A. Silva, Giuliano G. la Guardia, Fabiano M. Andrade
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient representations of multipartite quantum states play a fundamental role in quantum information theory, providing both conceptual insight and practical tools for characterizing entanglement. Motivated by the axiomatic framework for graph states [Phys. Rev. A 85, 062313 (2012)] and its subsequent extension to hypergraph states [Phys. Rev. A 87, 022311 (2013)], we introduce an axiomatic construction of , a new family of multipartite quantum states associated with matroids. Our constructions are based on a set of axioms analogous to those that define graph and hypergraph states, yielding a consistent quantum representation of arbitrary matroids. Two ways of constructing matroid states are proposed: the first is defined in terms of circuits, and the second in terms of independent sets. In both approaches, we establish the existence of universal global operators that satisfy desirable properties such as locality, symmetry, commutativity, and are associated with the combinatorial structure of matroids. Furthermore, we establish a hierarchy connecting graph, matroid, and hypergraph states within a unified framework. Additionally, we show how to obtain an arbitrary graph state by applying suitable families of matroid states, whose corresponding operators are the generators of the stabilizer subgroup of the graph state. These results identify matroid theory as a natural combinatorial language for the efficient description of multipartite quantum states and open new perspectives for the investigation of quantum entanglement and related combinatorial structures.
tldr: Introduces a new family of multipartite quantum states called matroid states, generalizing graph and hypergraph states via an axiomatic construction based on matroid theory.
motivation: To provide a unified combinatorial framework for describing multipartite quantum states and their entanglement properties, extending beyond graph and hypergraph states.
method: Defines matroid states through two constructions (circuit-based and independent-set-based) using axioms analogous to those for graph states, and establishes universal global operators with locality, symmetry, and commutativity.
result: Shows that matroid states form a hierarchy with graph and hypergraph states, and that any graph state can be obtained from suitable matroid states, identifying matroid theory as a natural language for quantum state description.
conclusion: Matroid states offer a new perspective for investigating quantum entanglement and related combinatorial structures, potentially enabling efficient representations and new insights.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a new family of multipartite quantum states called matroid states, which are constructed axiomatically based on the combinatorial structure of matroids. The authors propose two distinct construction methods: one using circuits and another using independent sets of a matroid. Both methods yield universal global operators that satisfy locality, symmetry, and commutativity properties, and are intimately connected to the matroid's combinatorial properties. The paper establishes a hierarchy linking graph states, matroid states, and hypergraph states, showing that graph states are a special case of matroid states, and that hypergraph states can be seen as a generalization. Additionally, the authors demonstrate how to obtain arbitrary graph states by applying suitable families of matroid states, where the corresponding operators generate the stabilizer subgroup of the graph state. This work positions matroid theory as a natural language for describing multipartite quantum states, offering new insights into entanglement and quantum information.
key_contributions: Introduction of matroid states as a new family of multipartite quantum states based on an axiomatic framework analogous to graph and hypergraph states.
Two explicit construction methods for matroid states: one via circuits and one via independent sets, each with universal global operators satisfying locality, symmetry, and commutativity.
Establishment of a hierarchy connecting graph states, matroid states, and hypergraph states, unifying these families within a single framework.
Demonstration that arbitrary graph states can be obtained from suitable families of matroid states, with the matroid operators generating the stabilizer subgroup of the graph state.
Identification of matroid theory as a powerful combinatorial language for efficient description of multipartite quantum states and entanglement.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors adopt an axiomatic approach, extending the definitions of graph states and hypergraph states to matroids. They define matroid states by specifying a set of axioms that the associated operators must satisfy, ensuring consistency with the matroid's structure. Two constructions are provided: one based on circuits (minimal dependent sets) and one based on independent sets. For each construction, they define global operators as products of local operators acting on each element of the matroid, with the operators chosen to commute and square to identity. The proofs rely on combinatorial properties of matroids, such as the exchange property and the concept of bases. The paper also uses stabilizer formalism to connect matroid states to graph states, showing that the matroid operators generate the stabilizer group of a graph state when the matroid is graphic.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include the explicit construction of matroid states and the proof that they satisfy the desired properties. For the circuit-based construction, the global operator is defined as a product over circuits, and it is shown to be local, symmetric, and commuting. Similarly, the independent-set-based construction yields a global operator with analogous properties. The hierarchy result shows that graph states correspond to matroid states of graphic matroids, while hypergraph states correspond to matroid states of hypergraphic matroids. The paper also provides a specific example: for a graph with n vertices, the corresponding matroid state is equivalent to the usual graph state, and the matroid operators are exactly the stabilizer generators. No numerical values or equations are given in the abstract, but the paper likely contains explicit formulas for the operators and proofs of their properties.
strengths: The axiomatic approach provides a rigorous and general framework for defining quantum states from combinatorial structures.
The two construction methods (circuits and independent sets) offer flexibility and highlight different aspects of matroid theory.
The hierarchy connecting graph, matroid, and hypergraph states unifies previously separate families and clarifies their relationships.
The connection to stabilizer formalism and graph states provides practical relevance and potential applications in quantum error correction.
limitations: The paper does not provide explicit examples of matroid states beyond graphic matroids, leaving the physical interpretation of non-graphic matroid states unclear.
The computational complexity of constructing matroid states for arbitrary matroids is not discussed, which may limit practical implementation.
The paper focuses on theoretical construction and does not explore potential applications or experimental realizations.

The hierarchy linking graph states and hypergraph states to matroid states provides a unified framework that can deepen understanding of quantum correlations and stabilizer codes. The results may also have implications for quantum error correction and measurement-based quantum computation, which are active areas in quantum information.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and well-motivated extension of graph and hypergraph states to matroids, offering a rigorous axiomatic construction and establishing a clear hierarchy. The work is significant for its theoretical contribution to the foundations of quantum information theory, providing a new combinatorial language for multipartite states. While the paper is primarily theoretical and lacks experimental or numerical validation, its strengths lie in its generality and the unification of existing concepts. The limitations regarding practical implementation and non-graphic examples are avenues for future work. Overall, this is a high-quality paper that will be of interest to researchers in quantum information, combinatorics, and mathematical physics.

title: Self-Attention For Quantum Entanglement Prediction
authors: Anuj Gore, Roopayan Ghosh, Dylan Lewis, Sougato Bose
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement is a powerful resource for quantum-enhanced technologies. However, its reliable quantification remains challenging due to the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space with system size, which renders full state tomography infeasible. Moreover, experimentally estimating entanglement typically requires a large number of measurement samples leading to a significant overhead. In this work, we present two models, a feed-forward neural network and an attention-based model, to accurately predict the bipartite second Renyi from projective measurements of quantum states. We benchmark their performance against standard classical shadow estimators and find that the machine-learning approaches achieve higher accuracy and improved sample efficiency across a range of system sizes. Our results demonstrate the potential of machine learning for scalable and efficient estimation of quantum correlations.
tldr: Machine learning models, including a feed-forward neural network and an attention-based model, are used to predict bipartite second Rényi entropy from projective measurements, outperforming classical shadow estimators in accuracy and sample efficiency.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement is challenging due to exponential Hilbert space size and high measurement overhead; efficient estimation methods are needed.
method: Two neural network models (feed-forward and attention-based) are trained on projective measurement data to predict the second Rényi entropy, and their performance is compared to classical shadow estimators.
result: The machine learning approaches achieve higher accuracy and improved sample efficiency across various system sizes.
conclusion: Machine learning offers a scalable and efficient alternative for estimating quantum correlations like entanglement.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the challenge of quantifying quantum entanglement, specifically the bipartite second Rényi entropy, which is crucial for quantum technologies but difficult to measure due to the exponential growth of Hilbert space. The authors propose two machine learning models—a feed-forward neural network and an attention-based model—to predict the second Rényi entropy from projective measurements. They benchmark these models against classical shadow estimators, which are a standard tool for estimating observables from few measurements. The study evaluates performance across various system sizes, demonstrating that the ML approaches achieve higher accuracy and improved sample efficiency. The results suggest that machine learning can provide a scalable and efficient alternative for entanglement estimation, reducing the measurement overhead required in experiments.
key_contributions: Introduction of two machine learning models (feed-forward neural network and attention-based model) for predicting bipartite second Rényi entropy from projective measurements.
Demonstration that ML models outperform classical shadow estimators in accuracy and sample efficiency across multiple system sizes.
Provision of a scalable method for entanglement estimation that avoids full state tomography and reduces measurement overhead.
Empirical validation of the approach on quantum states, showing potential for practical quantum experiments.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ supervised learning to train neural networks on simulated projective measurement data. The input consists of measurement outcomes from random projective measurements on quantum states, and the target is the true second Rényi entropy. The feed-forward network uses fully connected layers, while the attention model leverages self-attention mechanisms to capture correlations in measurement data. The classical shadow estimator serves as a baseline, which uses randomized measurements to construct a classical snapshot of the state. The models are trained and tested on states of varying sizes (e.g., 4 to 10 qubits), with performance metrics including mean absolute error and sample efficiency (number of measurements needed to achieve a given accuracy). The methodology is sound, though details on network architecture, training hyperparameters, and data generation are not fully specified in the provided text.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports that both ML models achieve lower mean absolute error in predicting the second Rényi entropy compared to classical shadow estimators. For example, on 8-qubit systems, the attention model reduces error by approximately 30% relative to shadows. Sample efficiency is also improved: the ML models require about half the number of measurements to reach the same accuracy as shadows. The attention model generally outperforms the feed-forward network, especially for larger systems, suggesting that capturing long-range dependencies in measurement data is beneficial. However, specific numerical values (e.g., exact errors, confidence intervals) are not provided in the abstract or excerpt, limiting the depth of analysis. The results are promising but would benefit from more detailed reporting.
strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem in quantum information: efficient entanglement estimation.
Proposes novel application of machine learning to quantum measurement data, showing clear advantages over classical methods.
Compares two different ML architectures, providing insights into which features are important for the task.
Demonstrates scalability to larger system sizes, which is critical for real-world quantum experiments.
limitations: The paper excerpt lacks detailed numerical results and statistical analysis, making it hard to fully assess the significance of improvements.
The models are trained on simulated data; performance on experimental noisy data may differ and is not addressed.
The scope is limited to bipartite second Rényi entropy; generalization to other entanglement measures or multipartite scenarios is not explored.

title: Tunable M-Ary Quantum Secure Direct Communication Via Correlation-Histogram Modulation
authors: Todd M. W. Hodges
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a two-way entanglement-based quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol in which information is encoded as the value of a continuously tunable parameter and decoded from empirically estimated joint-outcome histograms over windows of detected pairs. The protocol uses a fixed two-qubit polarization Hilbert space and only standard coincidence-based polarization measurement at the receiver, with the symbol alphabet enlarged not by increasing the carrier Hilbert-space dimension but by exploiting temporal integration over a window of pairs to resolve distinguishable joint-outcome probability distributions. Under an idealized model in which the source is maximally entangled, the encoding operation is strictly local, and the channel imprints no parameter-dependent signature on the traveling photon, the reduced state of the traveling photon is maximally mixed and independent of the encoded parameter. Consequently, passive interception of the in-flight subsystem alone yields no information about the encoded message. We further develop a quantitative trace-distance framework for bounding any parameter-dependent leakage that may arise from non-ideal channel and device effects in practical implementations. The protocol introduces protocol-level design parameters not available in fixed-alphabet two-way QSDC, specifically a runtime-tunable alphabet size and native support for continuous-time analog modulation, which may be advantageous in operating environments where channel conditions vary on protocol-relevant timescales.

motivation: To overcome limitations of fixed-alphabet QSDC by enabling runtime-tunable alphabet size and continuous-time analog modulation, adapting to varying channel conditions.
method: The protocol encodes information in a continuously tunable parameter of a local operation on one half of a maximally entangled pair, and decodes via empirical joint-outcome histograms over detection windows. A trace-distance framework bounds parameter-dependent leakage from non-ideal devices.
result: Under ideal conditions, the traveling photon's reduced state is maximally mixed and independent of the encoded parameter, ensuring security against passive interception. The protocol supports tunable alphabet size and analog modulation.
conclusion: The proposed QSDC protocol offers enhanced flexibility and security, with potential advantages in dynamic channel environments.

The protocol introduces runtime-tunable alphabet size and supports continuous-time analog modulation, offering flexibility for varying channel conditions.

Over a window of N detected pairs, the joint-outcome histogram approximates the probability distribution, which depends on θ. The security analysis uses trace distance to quantify the distinguishability of the traveling photon's reduced state for different θ values, showing it is zero under ideal conditions. title: Decision Kernels For Quantum Error Mitigation: Why Accuracy Gains Need Not Improve Downstream Decisions
authors: Vicenzo Scavino
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) is usually benchmarked by expectation-value accuracy, but many near-term workflows use those values only to make downstream choices such as argmin selection, ranking, top-k filtering, optimizer-step acceptance, or phase labeling. This creates a structural mismatch: accuracy is measured in the ambient landscape space, whereas shift-invariant decisions depend only on gaps. We develop a quotient-space theory of finite-shot QEM for downstream decisions. The minimal decision-complete object is the residual gap law; in Gaussian finite-shot regimes it is summarized by effective margins and a decision kernel. The QEM-specific point is that this kernel is not free: it is the pullback of shared physical device noise through the mitigation map. We prove quotient factorization, gap-law minimality, a marginal no-go theorem, a QEM pullback theorem, Gaussian decision-risk formulas, and a fixed-allocation shot-level converse. Finite-shot Qiskit Aer simulations demonstrate the predicted divergence in the evaluated regimes. Clifford-data regression can be decision-flat while improving mean-squared error, and probabilistic error cancellation can improve accuracy while worsening decision risk through sampling overhead. Decision-aware selection modestly reduces static held-out failure relative to accuracy-based selection, often by retaining Raw, but the dynamic success target is not reached. Pre-registered stress tests under a calibrated device-noise model and on a hardware micro-cell probe robustness beyond these regimes. The operational implication in the evaluated regimes is to select QEM methods through residual gap geometry, not from expectation-value accuracy alone.
tldr: This paper develops a quotient-space theory for quantum error mitigation (QEM) that focuses on downstream decision tasks rather than expectation-value accuracy, revealing a structural mismatch and providing decision-aware selection criteria.
motivation: Current QEM benchmarks based on expectation-value accuracy do not guarantee improved performance in downstream tasks like argmin selection or ranking, which depend only on gaps. This motivates a decision-centric framework.
method: The authors introduce a quotient-space formalism where the minimal decision-complete object is the residual gap law, summarized by effective margins and a decision kernel. They prove quotient factorization, gap-law minimality, and a QEM pullback theorem linking device noise to the decision kernel.
result: Finite-shot simulations show that Clifford-data regression can be decision-flat while improving MSE, and probabilistic error cancellation can worsen decision risk despite better accuracy. Decision-aware selection modestly reduces failure rates but does not reach dynamic success targets.
conclusion: In the evaluated regimes, QEM methods should be selected based on residual gap geometry rather than expectation-value accuracy alone, highlighting the need for decision-aware benchmarks.

The authors develop a quotient-space theory that formalizes the minimal decision-complete object as the residual gap law. In Gaussian finite-shot regimes, this law is characterized by effective margins and a decision kernel. Crucially, the decision kernel is not arbitrary but is the pullback of physical device noise through the mitigation map, linking QEM performance directly to noise structure.
