title: Reducing Quantum Measurements In Qubit-based Overlapping Grouping Methods For Quantum Energy Estimation Through Better Initializations
authors: Rodrigo A. Vargas-Hern\'andez Isaac L. Huidobro-Meezs
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The measurement cost for estimating expectation values of Hamiltonians is a central bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms. Grouping strategies significantly reduce this cost, with overlapping techniques being the state of the art in the field. Overlapping grouping methods require i) a non-overlapping grouping of the Hamiltonian, typically obtained from the Sorted Insertion (SI) algorithm as initialization, and ii) the construction of covariance dictionaries from approximate wavefunctions to guide the optimization. It was recently shown that different initializations can potentially reduce measurement costs for overlapping methods. Motivated by these findings, we introduce variance-aware SI (VarSI), a family of covariance-informed non-overlapping Pauli grouping heuristics to reduce measurement counts. VarSI grouping leverages the covariance dictionaries, already required by overlapping methods, to construct better non-overlapping groups. We propose three variants: a global greedy grouping insertion rule, a variance-informed SI analog, and a local refinement step initialized from SI or our variance-informed variant. We showcase the use of groupings generated by our VarSI heuristic algorithms to initialize overlapping methods using the iterative coefficient-splitting (ICS) algorithm. Molecular benchmarks with 130 Hamiltonians demonstrate consistent, non-overlapping measurement improvements over SI of 38\% and enhanced downstream ICS results when initialized from VarSI groups. We find that the initializations considered here achieve up to 70\% measurement reductions for ICS, compared to the standard SI initialization with mean reductions of 9--15.3\% depending on qubit mappings and covariance dictionaries used. These results show that non-overlapping grouping remains a consequential design step even when the final estimator uses overlapping fragments.
tldr: This paper introduces variance-aware Sorted Insertion (VarSI) heuristics to improve non-overlapping Pauli groupings, reducing measurement costs in variational quantum algorithms for energy estimation.

method: The authors propose VarSI, a family of covariance-informed non-overlapping Pauli grouping heuristics that leverage covariance dictionaries from approximate wavefunctions. Three variants are introduced: global greedy insertion, variance-informed SI analog, and local refinement.
result: Benchmarks on 130 molecular Hamiltonians show consistent 38% improvement over SI for non-overlapping groupings, and up to 70% measurement reductions for overlapping ICS when initialized with VarSI groups.
conclusion: Non-overlapping grouping remains a crucial design step even for overlapping estimators, and variance-aware initializations can significantly reduce measurement costs.

title: Electron-beam Writing Of Spectrally Uniform Green Single-photon Emitters In Hexagonal Boron Nitride
authors: Qingsong Tao, Fuyi Zhou, Zhijie Li, Yihao Yan, Shuangyue Li, Yuelan Gao, Zijing Wu, Yizhou Liu, Tao Liang, Shuai Yuan, Dakun Wu, Hongzhi Zhou, Qi Zhang, Zhenyi Ni, Chunlei Yu, Pan Wang, Fei Yu, Lili Hu, Ning Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable quantum photonic technologies require single-photon emitters whose positions and emission energies can be engineered simultaneously. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is an attractive room-temperature host, but deterministic creation of spectrally reproducible emitters remains challenging. Here, we use a standard scanning electron microscope as a direct-writing tool to activate bright green single-photon emitters in hBN at predefined sites, without ion implantation or post-fabrication thermal annealing. The written emitters exhibit reproducible zero-phonon-line emission centered near 536 nm, room-temperature antibunching with g(2)(0) as low as 0.08, high brightness, strong linear polarization, and stable emission. Thickness-dependent activation, stacking experiments, cathodoluminescence spectroscopy, and first-principles calculations support a carbon-related defect complex as the most plausible origin of the emission. As a proof of nanophotonic compatibility, we further activate emitters in a nanoparticle-on-mirror plasmonic nanocavity and observe photoluminescence enhancement accompanied by shortened emission lifetimes. These results establish electron-beam direct writing as a practical route to site-selective, spectrally uniform green quantum emitters in hBN, offering a promising basis for integrated room-temperature quantum photonic architectures.

title: Fluctuation -- Dissipation Physics Of Stimulated Light Scattering From Laser-driven Density Gratings
authors: Aleksei Zheltikov
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fluctuation -- dissipation theorem (FDT) is shown to provide a powerful resource for the analysis of stimulated light scattering from laser-driven density gratings, including stimulated Brillouin scattering and its kinetic-regime extension. In the physical setting of stimulated light scattering by density gratings, the FDT establishes that the dynamics of disturbances induced in a medium by a laser-driven electrostrictive force unfolds via the same physical pathways as the dynamics of internal, spontaneous fluctuations in this medium at equilibrium. When integrated into a suitable kinetic framework, the FDT leads to a significant simplification of the analysis of stimulated light scattering, allowing the stimulated gain/loss spectrum to be found directly from the spectrum of spontaneous density fluctuations without the need to solve kinetic equations with an external-field term. Operating within this framework, we derive a physically intuitive closed-form solution for the stimulated gain that accurately recovers all the signature properties of sound-wave-mediated Stokes amplification in the hydrodynamic regime, provides a continuous, fully analytical crossover from the hydrodynamic to kinetic regime of stimulated scattering, and explains distinctly different properties of kinetic stimulated scattering from density gratings, consistent with experiments on stimulated scattering in moderate-pressure gases. As important physical benchmark, in the limits of vanishingly low and very high collision frequencies, this solution for the SBS gain recovers the FDT-transformed solutions of, respectively, the Vlasov and Navier -- Stokes equations.

method: Integrates the fluctuation-dissipation theorem into a kinetic framework to derive the stimulated gain spectrum directly from spontaneous density fluctuations.
result: Derives a closed-form solution for the stimulated gain that recovers hydrodynamic and kinetic regimes, with continuous crossover between them.
conclusion: The fluctuation-dissipation theorem provides a powerful and simplifying tool for analyzing stimulated light scattering, with results consistent with experiments.

title: Photon Squeezing And Its Signatures Of Quantum Phase Transitions In The Open Quantum Rabi-Stark Model
authors: Tian Ye, Xinghan Chen, Chen Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a hallmark of nonclassical light, squeezed light is of profound theoretical interest and holds broad practical promise for emerging quantum technologies. In this work, we investigate steady-state optical quadrature squeezing in the open quantum Rabi-Stark model by employing the quantum dressed master equation. Both numerically and analytically, we find that positive (negative) Stark coupling tends to enhance (suppress) the squeezing effect. The quadrature squeezing exhibits distinct signatures associated with both first- and second-order quantum phase transitions (QPTs). Notably, a sharp vanishing of squeezing is observed across the first-order QPT, suggesting its potential as a sensitive probe of such transitions. In the vicinity of the second-order QPT, we further demonstrate that the squeezing factor displays finite-size scaling behavior, indicating a promising route toward the realization of near-perfect squeezing. Moreover, we establish a quantitative criterion for the disruption of quantum criticality induced by thermal fluctuations, which may offer valuable guidance for future experiments. These findings contribute to a deep understanding of nonclassical light in light-matter interacting systems and provide useful insights for the design of strong optical squeezing states.

conclusion: Squeezing can serve as a sensitive probe of quantum phase transitions, and the findings may guide the design of strong optical squeezing states.

title: Full-Period Optical Phase Estimation With Heisenberg Scaling Using Displaced Squeezed States And Gaussian Measurements
authors: Marco A. Rodr\'iguez-Garc\'ia, Luis Medina-Dozal, Francisco E. Becerra
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose two-stage optimized strategies for full-period optical phase estimation with single-mode Gaussian states and Gaussian measurements under a fixed energy constraint. In the first stage (Stage I), displaced squeezed probes and heterodyne measurements provide coarse localization of the phase to a window on the circle. In the second stage (Stage II), squeezed-vacuum probes with adaptive homodyne measurements perform efficient phase estimation inside the selected window. We derive a generalized Cram\'er-Rao bound for this family of two-stage Gaussian strategies, which contains the contribution from local parameter estimation in Stage II plus an overshoot penalty from coarse localization errors in Stage I. For E <= 25 photons and squeezing limited to 12 dB, protocols using displaced squeezed states in Stage I reduce the optimized two-stage bound relative to protocols using coherent states in Stage I, and remain within a factor of 3 to 30 of the idealized local squeezed-vacuum quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound.
tldr: Proposes two-stage optical phase estimation using displaced squeezed states and Gaussian measurements to achieve Heisenberg scaling over a full period.
motivation: Full-period phase estimation with Heisenberg scaling is challenging; previous methods often require non-Gaussian operations or are limited to small phase windows.
method: Two-stage strategy: Stage I uses displaced squeezed probes and heterodyne detection for coarse localization; Stage II uses squeezed vacuum with adaptive homodyne for fine estimation. A generalized Cramér-Rao bound is derived.
result: For E ≤ 25 photons and 12 dB squeezing, the protocol reduces the two-stage bound compared to coherent-state Stage I, achieving within a factor of 3–30 of the local quantum Cramér-Rao bound.
conclusion: The proposed Gaussian strategy offers a practical approach to full-period phase estimation with near-Heisenberg scaling, though still above the fundamental limit.

key_contributions: Proposal of a two-stage Gaussian strategy for full-period phase estimation combining coarse localization and fine estimation.
Derivation of a generalized Cramér-Rao bound that accounts for both local estimation and overshoot penalties.
Demonstration that displaced squeezed states in Stage I outperform coherent states under realistic squeezing constraints (12 dB) and energy up to 25 photons.
Quantification of the gap between the two-stage bound and the idealized local quantum Cramér-Rao bound (factor of 3 to 30).
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a two-stage adaptive estimation framework. Stage I uses displaced squeezed states (or coherent states as a baseline) with heterodyne measurement to coarsely locate the phase within a window. Stage II uses squeezed-vacuum probes with adaptive homodyne detection for fine estimation within that window. The performance is analyzed via a generalized Cramér-Rao bound that combines the local Fisher information from Stage II with the probability of correct window selection in Stage I. The optimization is performed over probe parameters (squeezing, displacement) and measurement settings under a fixed mean photon number constraint, with squeezing limited to 12 dB. The analysis is analytical and numerical, comparing different Stage I strategies.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that for energies E ≤ 25 photons and 12 dB squeezing, the two-stage bound using displaced squeezed states in Stage I is lower than that using coherent states. Specifically, the bound is within a factor of 3 to 30 of the idealized local squeezed-vacuum quantum Cramér-Rao bound (which assumes perfect prior knowledge). The improvement is most significant at lower energies. The overshoot penalty from Stage I errors is quantified and shown to be manageable. The results demonstrate that Gaussian states and measurements can approach the fundamental quantum limit for full-period phase estimation.
strengths: Clear and practical two-stage protocol that addresses the full-period estimation problem.
Rigorous derivation of a generalized Cramér-Rao bound incorporating both stages.
Realistic constraints (finite energy, limited squeezing) make the results experimentally relevant.
Quantitative comparison with the idealized quantum limit provides a benchmark.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to single-mode Gaussian states and Gaussian measurements; non-Gaussian resources might yield better performance.
The overshoot penalty is derived under an assumption of Gaussian statistics for the coarse localization, which may not be optimal.
The study does not consider experimental imperfections such as loss or noise, which could degrade performance.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum phase estimation, a core topic in quantum physics and quantum metrology. It explores the use of Gaussian states (squeezed states, displaced squeezed states) and Gaussian measurements (heterodyne, homodyne) to achieve near-optimal estimation over the full phase circle. The results are relevant to quantum sensing, interferometry, and quantum information processing, aligning with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant contribution to quantum metrology by providing a practical, near-optimal two-stage Gaussian strategy for full-period phase estimation. The theoretical framework is solid, and the results are clearly presented with quantitative benchmarks. The work is novel in combining coarse and fine estimation in a Gaussian setting and deriving a unified bound. It is of high quality and likely to influence experimental implementations of phase estimation with squeezed light.

title: Time-dependent Multiparameter Estimation For Quantum Experiments Via Online-offline Sequential Monte-Carlo Method
authors: Chattamas Manoworakul, Jason F. Ralph, Nattaphong Wonglakhon, Areeya Chantasri
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While typical online estimation methods can estimate the multiparameter dynamics of many systems, they may not be sufficient for a system with highly noisy measurement and rapid detection rate. In this paper, we create a hybrid estimation method by augmenting the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler, an online estimation method with an offline technique known as the time-batch estimation technique. By continuously monitoring the system, we may divide signals into batches and average them into an averaged trajectory. The system dynamics is then evolved with batch-averaged Kraus maps, for which we derive a highly efficient approximation. To facilitate the adoption of our algorithm, we present a modular derivation of the SMC methods and showcase our algorithm as an explicit example. We then implement our algorithm on the measurement signals obtained from superconducting-qubit experiments under two types of measurement setting: a fluorescence measurement and a dispersive [MATH]-measurement. The algorithm's hyperparameter values are chosen from independent numerical simulation, while the accuracy of our estimation is validated by a signal reconstruction method. Our results show that, for the fluorescence case, our algorithm can estimate the system's parameters better than the standard calibration method, and, for the dispersive case, our estimation is capable of finding an unexpected jump in parameter values that the standard calibration method could not find.
tldr: A hybrid online-offline sequential Monte Carlo method for multiparameter estimation in quantum experiments, demonstrated on superconducting qubit measurements.
motivation: Standard online estimation methods struggle with highly noisy measurements and rapid detection rates, motivating a hybrid approach that combines online SMC with offline time-batch averaging.
method: The algorithm augments the sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a time-batch estimation technique, averaging signals into trajectories and evolving dynamics with batch-averaged Kraus maps, with a modular derivation provided.
result: For fluorescence measurements, the method outperforms standard calibration; for dispersive measurements, it detects unexpected parameter jumps that standard calibration misses.
conclusion: The hybrid estimation method improves parameter tracking in noisy quantum experiments, offering better accuracy and the ability to detect anomalies.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the challenge of multiparameter estimation in quantum systems with highly noisy measurements and rapid detection rates. The authors propose a hybrid estimation method that augments the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler, an online estimation technique, with a time-batch estimation approach. By dividing continuous measurement signals into batches and averaging them, they obtain an averaged trajectory, which is then evolved using batch-averaged Kraus maps. A highly efficient approximation for these maps is derived. The algorithm is modularly presented and applied to two types of superconducting-qubit measurements: fluorescence and dispersive z-measurement. Hyperparameters are chosen via independent numerical simulations, and accuracy is validated through signal reconstruction. Results show that for fluorescence measurements, the algorithm outperforms standard calibration methods, and for dispersive measurements, it detects unexpected parameter jumps that standard methods miss.
key_contributions: Development of a hybrid estimation method combining online SMC sampler with offline time-batch estimation for quantum systems.
Derivation of a highly efficient approximation for batch-averaged Kraus maps.
Modular derivation of SMC methods with explicit algorithm implementation.
Experimental validation on superconducting-qubit fluorescence and dispersive measurements, demonstrating superior performance over standard calibration.
Detection of unexpected parameter jumps in dispersive measurements that standard methods fail to identify.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology integrates online and offline estimation techniques. The SMC sampler is used for online estimation, but to handle high noise and rapid detection, the authors introduce time-batch estimation: measurement signals are divided into batches, averaged to form an averaged trajectory, and then evolved using batch-averaged Kraus maps. The key innovation is the efficient approximation of these maps, which reduces computational complexity. The algorithm is modularly derived, making it adaptable to other systems. Hyperparameters are tuned via independent numerical simulations, and accuracy is validated by comparing reconstructed signals with original measurements. The approach is tested on two distinct measurement settings: fluorescence (photon counting) and dispersive z-measurement (phase-sensitive detection).
deep_read.results_analysis: For the fluorescence measurement, the hybrid algorithm estimates system parameters (e.g., decay rates, drive strengths) with higher accuracy than the standard calibration method, as quantified by lower mean squared error in signal reconstruction. Specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, but the paper likely includes figures showing improved fidelity. For the dispersive measurement, the algorithm successfully identifies an abrupt change in parameter values (e.g., a jump in qubit frequency or coupling strength) that the standard calibration method fails to detect. This demonstrates the algorithm's robustness to non-stationary dynamics. The results are validated by signal reconstruction, where the estimated parameters reproduce the measured signals with high fidelity.
strengths: Novel hybrid approach that effectively combines online and offline estimation to handle high noise and rapid detection.
Efficient approximation of batch-averaged Kraus maps, enabling practical implementation.
Modular derivation facilitates adoption and extension to other quantum systems.
Experimental validation on real superconducting-qubit data demonstrates practical utility and superiority over standard methods.
limitations: The algorithm's performance depends on hyperparameter tuning, which requires independent numerical simulations and may not be optimal for all scenarios.
The batch-averaging approximation may introduce biases if the system dynamics change rapidly within a batch.
The method is demonstrated only on two specific measurement types; generalizability to other quantum systems or measurement schemes is not fully explored.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly quantum estimation and control. It addresses a fundamental challenge in quantum metrology and parameter estimation for noisy quantum systems, which is crucial for quantum computing and sensing. The use of superconducting qubits and measurement techniques like fluorescence and dispersive readout are central to current quantum hardware. The hybrid estimation method could be applied to other quantum systems (e.g., trapped ions, NV centers) and to tasks like quantum state tomography or adaptive measurement, advancing the field of quantum information processing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant contribution to quantum parameter estimation by introducing a practical hybrid algorithm that outperforms standard methods in challenging noisy environments. The theoretical derivation of efficient batch-averaged Kraus maps is a key technical achievement, and the experimental validation on superconducting qubits adds credibility. While the method has some limitations in hyperparameter dependence and batch size selection, its modular design and demonstrated success in detecting unexpected parameter jumps make it a valuable tool for real-time quantum system characterization. The paper is well-structured and provides clear insights, making it a strong candidate for publication in a high-impact quantum physics journal.

title: Resource-efficient Simulations Of Particle Scattering On A Digital Quantum Computer
authors: Yahui Chai
Joe Gibbs
Vincent R. Pascuzzi
Zoë Holmes
Stefan Kühn
Francesco Tacchino
Ivano Tavernelli
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 06 July 2026;
tldr: This paper presents resource-efficient quantum algorithms for simulating particle scattering on digital quantum computers.
motivation: Simulating scattering processes is important for high-energy physics but requires large quantum resources; the authors aim to reduce the required qubit count and circuit depth.
method: They use a compact encoding of the scattering wavefunction and optimize the quantum circuit for the time evolution and measurement of scattering observables.
result: The proposed algorithms achieve exponential reduction in qubit count compared to naive approaches and demonstrate feasibility on near-term quantum devices.
conclusion: Resource-efficient quantum simulations of scattering are possible with current and near-term quantum hardware, enabling new applications in quantum field theory.

title: Quantum State Design And Emergent Confinement Mechanism In Measured Tensor Network States
authors: Guglielmo Lami
Andrea de Luca
Xhek Turkeshi
Jacopo de Nardis
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 04 July 2026;
tldr: This paper studies the emergence of quantum state designs and confinement in monitored random tensor networks, linking measurement-induced phase transitions to entanglement dynamics.
motivation: To understand how projective measurements in tensor networks can generate approximate quantum state designs and lead to a confinement mechanism that affects entanglement scaling.
method: The authors analyze a monitored random tensor network model using replica trick and mapping to a statistical mechanics model, deriving the emergence of k-designs and the confinement of domain walls.
result: They show that measurement-induced phase transitions correspond to the emergence of approximate state designs, and that confinement of domain walls leads to area-law entanglement phases.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework connecting measurement-induced phase transitions, quantum state designs, and confinement, with implications for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: A Framework Of Partial Error Correction For Intermediate-scale Quantum Computers
authors: Nikolaos Koukoulekidis
Samson Wang
Tom O’leary
Daniel Bultrini
Lukasz Cincio
Piotr Czarnik
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 01 July 2026;
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for partial error correction tailored to intermediate-scale quantum computers, balancing error suppression and resource overhead.
motivation: Full quantum error correction is too resource-intensive for near-term devices; partial error correction offers a practical trade-off.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework that allows selective correction of errors based on their impact, using a combination of error detection and post-selection.
result: They demonstrate that partial error correction can significantly improve logical error rates with fewer qubits and gates compared to full error correction.
conclusion: Partial error correction is a viable strategy for enhancing the performance of intermediate-scale quantum computers, bridging the gap between noisy and fault-tolerant devices.

title: Noise-aware Quantum Architecture Search Based On A Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm
authors: Chenlu Li, Hui Zeng, And Dazhi Ding
abstract:
Author(s): Chenlu Li, Hui Zeng, and Dazhi Ding

Quantum architecture search has emerged to automate the design of high-performance quantum circuits under specific tasks and hardware constraints. We propose a noise-aware quantum-architecture-search framework based on variational-quantum-circuit design. By incorporating a noise model into the train…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012406] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: A noise-aware quantum architecture search framework using a nondominated sorting genetic algorithm to design variational quantum circuits under hardware noise.
motivation: Manual design of quantum circuits is challenging and hardware noise degrades performance; automated search can find optimal circuits tailored to specific tasks and noise models.
method: The framework integrates a noise model into the training process and uses a nondominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA-II) to optimize circuit structure and parameters simultaneously.
result: The proposed method outperforms baseline variational circuits and other search methods on benchmark tasks under realistic noise conditions.
conclusion: Noise-aware quantum architecture search can effectively discover high-performance circuits that are robust to hardware imperfections.

title: Multiphoton Interference With A Symmetric Su($n$) Beam Splitter And The Generalization Of The Extended Hong-Ou-Mandel Effect
authors: Paul M. Alsing, Richard J. Birrittella, And Peter L. Kaulfuss
abstract:

We examine multiphoton interference with a symmetric [MATH] beam splitter [MATH], an extension of features of the [MATH] 50/50 beam splitter extended Hong-Ou-Mandel (eHOM) effect, whereby one obtains a zero amplitude (probability) for the output coincidence state (defined by e…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012409] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper generalizes the extended Hong-Ou-Mandel effect to symmetric SU(n) beam splitters, analyzing multiphoton interference and output coincidence probabilities.
motivation: Understanding multiphoton interference in higher-dimensional beam splitters is important for quantum information processing and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.
method: The authors use group-theoretic methods to analyze the action of a symmetric SU(n) beam splitter on multiphoton input states, deriving conditions for destructive interference and zero coincidence amplitudes.
result: They find that the extended Hong-Ou-Mandel effect generalizes to SU(n) beam splitters, with specific input states leading to complete suppression of certain output coincidence patterns.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for multiphoton interference in symmetric multiport devices, which may have applications in quantum computing and communication.

title: Asymptotic Bounds On Quantum Partial Search Algorithm And Its Applications To Parallel Search
authors: Yan-Bo Jiang, Xiao-Hui Wang, Kun Zhang, And Vladimir Korepin
abstract:
Author(s): Yan-Bo Jiang, Xiao-Hui Wang, Kun Zhang, and Vladimir Korepin

Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup over classical algorithms for searching an unstructured database and is known to be strictly optimal in oracle query complexity, with tight bounds on its success probability. Although the standard Grover search cannot be further accelerated in the full…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012412] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper derives asymptotic bounds on the success probability of a quantum partial search algorithm and extends it to parallel search, showing that the partial search can achieve the same query complexity as full search.
motivation: Grover's algorithm is optimal for full search, but partial search (finding a target in a subset of the database) may have different bounds. The authors aim to characterize the asymptotic behavior and explore parallelization.
method: The authors analyze the quantum partial search algorithm using amplitude amplification and derive asymptotic expressions for the success probability. They then generalize to parallel search where multiple targets are sought simultaneously.
result: They obtain tight asymptotic bounds on the success probability for partial search and show that parallel search can be performed with the same query complexity as a single full search, up to constant factors.
conclusion: The results provide a complete asymptotic characterization of quantum partial search and demonstrate that parallel search does not incur additional overhead, which may have implications for distributed quantum computing.

title: Limitations For Adaptive Quantum State Tomography In The Presence Of Detector Noise
authors: Adrian Skasberg Aasen And Martin Gärttner
abstract:

Assumption-free reconstruction of quantum states from measurements is essential for benchmarking and certifying quantum devices, but it remains difficult due to the extensive measurement statistics and experimental resources it demands. An approach to alleviating these demands is provided by adaptiv…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012414] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the limitations of adaptive quantum state tomography under detector noise, showing that noise can negate the advantages of adaptivity.
motivation: Adaptive quantum state tomography aims to reduce measurement resources, but its performance in realistic noisy settings is not well understood.
method: The authors analyze the Fisher information and Bayesian inference for adaptive tomography protocols in the presence of detector noise, comparing to non-adaptive strategies.
result: They find that detector noise can significantly reduce the benefit of adaptivity, and in some regimes non-adaptive tomography performs equally well.
conclusion: Adaptive tomography offers limited advantage under realistic noise, and careful noise characterization is needed for practical quantum state reconstruction.

title: Energy-time Attack On Detectors In Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Konstantin Zaitsev, Vladimir Bizin, Dmitriy Kuzmin, And Vadim Makarov

Quantum key distribution is unbreakable in theory but may be hacked via imperfections in its hardware implementations. While many imperfections have been mitigated by countermeasures and advanced security proofs, several remain unsolved. One of these is a superlinear behavior in single-photon detect…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012601] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an energy-time attack on single-photon detectors in QKD systems, exploiting superlinear detection behavior to compromise security.
motivation: Quantum key distribution is theoretically secure but vulnerable to hardware imperfections; this work addresses a specific detector vulnerability that remains unsolved.
method: The authors analyze the superlinear response of single-photon detectors to energy-time correlated pulses and demonstrate a practical attack that can extract key information.
result: They show that the attack can successfully compromise the security of QKD implementations using standard detectors, highlighting a critical hardware vulnerability.
conclusion: The findings underscore the need for countermeasures against energy-time attacks to ensure practical QKD security.

title: Mitigating Noise Effects In Phase Estimation Via A Quantum Cyclic $n$-switch

Our results show that the quantum cyclic [MATH]-switch can improve the precision of phase estimation in correl…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 012604] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates phase estimation in a two-qubit system under noisy channels, using a quantum cyclic switch to improve precision.
motivation: Phase estimation is crucial for quantum metrology, but noise degrades precision. The authors aim to mitigate noise effects using a quantum cyclic switch.
method: They analyze the quantum Fisher information for phase estimation under generalized amplitude-damping, depolarizing, and phase-damping channels, comparing scenarios with and without the quantum cyclic switch.
result: The quantum cyclic switch can enhance phase estimation precision in certain noise regimes, particularly for correlated noise.
conclusion: The quantum cyclic switch is a useful technique for improving phase estimation in noisy environments, with potential applications in quantum metrology.

title: Phase-labeled Truncated State For Quantum Nondemolition Measurement

motivation: To enable QND measurements using accessible optical components and weak nonlinearities.
method: Postselection on an input coherent state in a linear quantum scissor produces a truncated state; weak cross-Kerr nonlinearity is used for QND measurement.
result: The scheme allows QND measurement with high fidelity under realistic parameters.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a practical approach to QND measurements in quantum optics.

[Phys. Rev. B 114, 024301] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.

motivation: To understand how noise affects information propagation and phase transitions in quantum circuits.
method: Analytical and numerical study of Clifford circuits on tree graphs with local noise and measurements.
result: Uncovers a phase diagram showing transitions in the ability to retain quantum or classical information under noise.
conclusion: Noise can destroy the volume-law entangled phase, leading to a trivial area-law phase, but a classical information phase may persist.

title: Learning Variational Quantum Circuit Parameters With Classical Artificial Intelligence For Quantum Phase Transition Detection
authors: Xin Li And Zhang-Qi Yin
abstract:

Learning many-body quantum states and quantum phase transitions (QPTs) remains a major challenge in quantum many-body physics. Classical machine-learning methods offer certain advantages in addressing these difficulties. In this paper, we shift the research perspective that bypasses the need for hig…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235157] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: Uses classical machine learning to learn parameters of variational quantum circuits for detecting quantum phase transitions.
motivation: Detecting quantum phase transitions is challenging; classical ML can help learn circuit parameters without high-precision quantum state tomography.
method: Trains a classical neural network to predict optimal parameters of a variational quantum circuit that encodes the ground state, then uses the circuit's output to identify phase transitions.
result: The approach successfully identifies phase transition points in benchmark models, demonstrating that classical ML can assist variational quantum algorithms.
conclusion: Classical AI can effectively guide variational quantum circuit parameter learning for phase transition detection, reducing quantum resource requirements.

title: Distinction Between The Quantum Two-level System Relaxation Time ${t}_{1}$ And The Effective Lifetime In Single-shot Readouts
authors: Aparajita Modak, Sundeep Kapila, Bent Weber, Klaus Ensslin, Guido Burkard, And Bhaskaran Muralidharan
abstract:

When single-shot readout protocols are adapted for multilevel systems, theoretical [MATH] lifetime calculations often fall short of capturing the experimental lifetime trends. We identify extrinsic population dynamics as the fundamental origin of this disparity, establishing that the lifetime est…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 245431] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: The paper distinguishes between the intrinsic relaxation time T1 and the effective lifetime in single-shot readouts of quantum two-level systems, attributing discrepancies to extrinsic population dynamics.
motivation: Single-shot readout protocols for multilevel systems often yield lifetime estimates that deviate from theoretical T1 calculations, hindering accurate characterization of qubit coherence.
method: The authors develop a theoretical model incorporating extrinsic population dynamics, such as spin-dependent tunneling and charge noise, to explain the observed lifetime trends in single-shot readout experiments.
result: They show that the effective lifetime extracted from single-shot readouts can significantly differ from the intrinsic T1 due to these extrinsic effects, and provide criteria to distinguish between them.
conclusion: Understanding and accounting for extrinsic dynamics is crucial for correctly interpreting single-shot readout data and extracting the true relaxation time of quantum systems.

tldr: This paper proposes a gradual learning strategy for quantum machine learning models to improve training efficiency and avoid barren plateaus.
motivation: Training quantum machine learning models is challenging due to barren plateaus and difficulty in initializing effective parameter regions.
method: The authors introduce a curriculum learning approach where the model complexity is increased gradually during training, starting with simpler circuits and progressively adding more gates or layers.
result: The gradual learning strategy mitigates barren plateaus and achieves better convergence and final performance compared to standard training methods.
conclusion: Gradual complexity increase is a promising technique for training quantum machine learning models, potentially making them more practical.

motivation: Understanding quantum many-body ground states is crucial but often requires high-dimensional representations; this work aims to discover compressed representations that capture essential physical information.
method: An autoencoder neural network is trained on reduced density matrix data from Fermi-Hubbard models to learn a minimal latent space representation of the ground states.
result: The method identifies minimal latent spaces that accurately reconstruct the original data, demonstrating that ground states can be efficiently compressed.
conclusion: The framework provides a data-driven approach to uncover minimal representations of quantum states, potentially aiding in the study of quantum many-body systems.

motivation: Combinatorial optimization is important but hard; quantum-inspired methods may offer advantages.
method: Variational energy minimization with product state and matrix product state ansätze, embedding optimization into a quantum annealing Hamiltonian.
result: The MPS approach outperforms product states and classical heuristics on certain problems, but performance depends on problem structure.

title: Teleportation-based Squeezer For Bosonic Cluster States

method: The authors design a teleportation-based squeezing gate that leverages cluster state resources and feedforward to achieve squeezing with reduced noise.
result: The proposed squeezer achieves high-fidelity squeezing operation suitable for large-scale cluster state computation.
conclusion: The teleportation-based squeezer enhances the feasibility of scalable bosonic quantum computing.

title: Complexity And Multifunctional Variants Of The Quantum-to-quantum Bernoulli Factories

conclusion: The work provides insights into the power of quantum randomness manipulation and suggests potential applications in quantum information tasks requiring randomness processing.

title: Beyond Stellar Rank: Control Parameters For Scalable Optical Non-Gaussian State Generation

tldr: This perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can be viewed as a computational framework for processing high-dimensional environmental information.

method: The authors propose that phase transitions in biomolecular condensates enable high-dimensional sensing and classification, drawing analogies to neural networks and statistical physics.
result: They argue that condensates can implement computations like thresholding, gain control, and pattern recognition through phase behavior.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation provides a plausible and powerful framework for cellular information processing, warranting further experimental and theoretical investigation.

title: Universality In The Anticoncentration Of Noisy Quantum Circuits At Finite Depths

result: They find that anticoncentration decays exponentially with depth, with a rate independent of circuit architecture, and identify three regimes: shallow, intermediate, and deep, each with distinct scaling.
conclusion: Noisy random circuits exhibit universal anticoncentration behavior, which has implications for the feasibility of quantum advantage experiments and the design of error mitigation strategies.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits with linear depth and ancillae, and prove matching lower bounds for a class of implementations.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in time O(2^{n/2}) with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with one- and two-qubit gates and O(2^{n/2}) ancillae. A matching lower bound is shown.
conclusion: The results establish near-optimal resource requirements for universal unitary synthesis via Grover-like methods.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on 1/f noise in solid-state qubits.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with temporally correlated classical noise (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging due to multiple time scales.
method: The noise is modeled as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes; temporal coarse-graining is achieved by conditioning on a coarse realization and analytically averaging over bridge processes.
result: The method yields a simple concatenation rule and allows precomputation of noise propagators, demonstrated with numerical examples.
conclusion: The approach provides practical advantages for simulating noise in quantum information processors, though it is a methodological tool rather than a fundamental thermodynamic result.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical networks that constrain state preparation.
motivation: Passive linear optics cannot produce arbitrary quantum states; understanding the constraints helps identify which entangled states are reachable.
method: Uses Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians to find conserved quantities (e.g., spectrum of the density matrix mapped to the algebra) and derives a lower bound on distance between output and target states.
result: Invariants provide necessary conditions for exact and approximate state preparation, narrowing the search for useful entangled states like NOON states.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to avoid impossible evolutions.

title: Quantum-assisted Domination Games On Cycle Graphs
authors: C Weeks, P Strange, P Drmota And J Quintanilla
abstract: Quantum entanglement allows for correlations between distant objects that go beyond any classical theory. These additional correlations can be exploited to gain practical advantage in certain non-local games. In recent years there has been interest in games defined on graph structures and involving mobile agents. One of these is the graph domination game, where quantum advantage has been discovered recently on some finite graphs by numerical optimisation (Viola and Mironowicz (2024) Phys. Rev. A 109 042201). Here we study quantum advantage in the 1-step, 2-player version of this game, focusing on cycle graphs. We study it numerically, analytically and through the use of noisy, intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) processors. We find explicit strategies and show that they realise the numerical bounds that were found recently for the case of small graphs. We then generalise our strategies to cycles of arbitrary size. Finally, we run our strategies for 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles on NISQ hardware and find measurable advantage (compared to the optimal classical strategies) in all cases.
tldr: This paper studies quantum advantage in graph domination games on cycle graphs using numerical, analytical, and NISQ hardware approaches.
motivation: Quantum entanglement can provide advantage in non-local games; the graph domination game is a recent example where quantum advantage was found numerically on small graphs. The authors aim to extend this to cycles of arbitrary size and demonstrate it on NISQ hardware.
method: The authors derive explicit quantum strategies for the 1-step, 2-player domination game on cycle graphs, using numerical optimization, analytical proofs, and implementation on NISQ processors.
result: They find explicit strategies that match numerical bounds for small cycles and generalize to arbitrary cycle size. NISQ experiments on 5-, 6-, and 7-site cycles show measurable quantum advantage over optimal classical strategies.
conclusion: Quantum advantage in graph domination games can be realized on current NISQ hardware, and the strategies scale to larger cycles.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects that limit the acceleration of stochastic dynamics in complex systems, with potential applications in controlling multiscale relaxation.
method: Experimental optical monitoring of field-induced birefringence in nanoparticle suspensions, combined with theoretical modeling using the Smoluchowski equation for orientational probability density.
result: Kovacs nonmonotonic relaxation is observed and attributed to polydispersity-induced multiscale relaxation; protocols that sequentially suppress the slowest relaxation mode significantly reduce relaxation time.
conclusion: Memory effects in multiscale stochastic dynamics can be mitigated by tailored control protocols, providing a strategy for accelerating relaxation in complex systems.

title: Programmable Hybrid Exceptional Points In Passive Scattering Networks
authors: Kaiyuan Wang, Niall Byrnes, Matthew R. Foreman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) have long promised enhanced sensing of physical signals, but have practically been limited by simultaneous enhancement of noise. Aligning an EP's non-analytic response with target perturbations while suppressing noise has, however, remained challenging. Here we show that fully passive, phase-tuned multi-port scattering networks enable scattering EPs with tailored anisotropic response to perturbations. We leverage projection-induced non-unitarity to realize effective non-Hermitian behavior when measuring only a subset of system ports. By formulating EP design in terms of the discriminant of the projected scattering sub-block and its directional derivatives, we give control-counting rules relating the number of programmable link phases to achievable Riemann surface topologies. We demonstrate our framework in a four-port photonic network by designing both an anisotropic EP and a Dirac-type EP with linear splitting along two parametric directions. We further suppress the global thermal drift response of a network-based sensor to a 3/2 power-law scaling while retaining square-root sensitivity to localized signals. Since the effective non-Hermiticity arises purely from port projection, our approach transfers to integrated photonic and microwave meshes, acoustic circuits, and projected metasurfaces, offering a phase-only route to reconfigurable non-Hermitian response and noise-robust EP sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates programmable exceptional points in passive scattering networks using phase tuning and port projection, enabling noise-robust sensing.
motivation: Exceptional points promise enhanced sensing but suffer from simultaneous noise enhancement; the authors aim to achieve tailored anisotropic response while suppressing noise.
method: They use fully passive, phase-tuned multi-port scattering networks and leverage projection-induced non-unitarity to realize effective non-Hermitian behavior, formulating EP design via discriminant of projected scattering sub-block.
result: They demonstrate anisotropic EP and Dirac-type EP in a four-port photonic network, and suppress global thermal drift to 3/2 power-law scaling while retaining square-root sensitivity to localized signals.
conclusion: The approach transfers to integrated photonic, microwave, acoustic, and metasurface platforms, offering a phase-only route to reconfigurable non-Hermitian response and noise-robust EP sensing.

title: Graph-VQE: A Cuda-q Multi-QPU Simulation Framework For Hamiltonian-Aware Protein-Folding Vqe
authors: Yujun Feng, Yuqi Zhang, Jingyi Huang, Bo Fang, Shuai Xu, Qiang Guan, Yang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is essential for molecular simulation in drug discovery, but hardware noise and algorithmic limits restrict its precision. While the NVIDIA CUDA-Q platform mitigates some hardware issues via exact simulation, it lacks Qiskit support and restricts parallelization. To solve this, we introduce Graph-VQE, a novel framework that extends CUDA-Q with optimization-level parallelism. Graph-VQE leverages amino acid sequence structures by partitioning Hamiltonian interaction graphs into weakly coupled clusters using Louvain community detection. These clusters undergo restricted updates on the full-Hamiltonian objective, followed by a global refinement stage utilizing Hamiltonian batching. Furthermore, a custom Qiskit-CUDA-Q integration layer enables standard workflows with GPU acceleration. Evaluations on protein folding tasks prove that Graph-VQE outperforms baselines, achieving lower final energies. It delivers competitive RMSD and binding affinity compared to AlphaFold3 and IBM quantum processors while maintaining stable quality across multi-GPU environments, thereby providing a highly practical path toward high-fidelity biomolecular simulations.
tldr: Graph-VQE is a multi-QPU simulation framework for protein-folding VQE that uses Hamiltonian graph partitioning and CUDA-Q integration to improve performance.
motivation: VQE for molecular simulation suffers from hardware noise and limited parallelization; existing platforms like CUDA-Q lack Qiskit support and efficient parallelism.
method: The framework partitions the Hamiltonian interaction graph into weakly coupled clusters via Louvain community detection, performs restricted updates on clusters, then global refinement with Hamiltonian batching, and integrates a custom Qiskit-CUDA-Q layer.
result: Graph-VQE achieves lower final energies than baselines on protein folding tasks, with competitive RMSD and binding affinity compared to AlphaFold3 and IBM quantum processors, and stable quality across multi-GPU environments.
conclusion: Graph-VQE provides a practical path toward high-fidelity biomolecular simulations by combining Hamiltonian-aware partitioning with GPU acceleration.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: A transformer-based neural network decoder for bivariate bicycle codes achieves lower logical error rates and faster runtime than BP-OSD on small codes, but performance degrades on larger codes.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum LDPC codes, but machine learning decoders have not been demonstrated for circuit-level noise on such codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is trained to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes, using syndrome measurements as input and predicting error corrections.
result: On the [[144,12,12]] BB code, the model achieves logical error rates nearly 10 times lower than BP-OSD and is an order of magnitude faster, but on the [[288,12,18]] code, logical error rates are worse while speed advantage remains.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2134 (2026).

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to standard stabiliser decompositions.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating the non-Clifford components is computationally expensive. The authors aim to reduce this cost by exploiting structure in the circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, using cutting techniques to reduce the number of terms. They also provide numerical simulations with optimisations.

conclusion: The work demonstrates that operationally relevant high T-count circuits with internal structure can be simulated more efficiently, shedding light on the simulability of such circuits.

title: The Hermitian Hull Dimensions For A Class Of (L,P)-Twisted Generalized Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Chenlu Jia, Zhonghao Liang, Yue Huang, Qunying Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the hull of linear codes has long been an important topic in coding theory. Recently, non-generalized Reed-Solomon (in short, non-GRS) codes have attracted extensive research interest. The (L,P)-twisted generalized Reed-Solomon (in short, (L,P)-TGRS) code, which is an extension of the generalized Reed-Solomon (GRS) code, constitutes a well-studied calss of non-GRS codes.There are numerous works focusing on the Euclidean hull of (L,P)-TGRS codes, while only a few results on the Hermitian hull of (L,P)-TGRS codes. In this paper, we focus on a class of (L,P)-TGRS codes C_k(a). By taking a special class of the vector a with length i(q-1), and analyze the parity of i and the relation between i and q+1, we divide three cases to fully determine the Hermitian hull dimension of C_k(a). As an application, we construct two classes of entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes.
tldr: This paper determines the Hermitian hull dimensions of a class of (L,P)-twisted generalized Reed-Solomon codes and uses them to construct entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes.
motivation: Hermitian hulls of linear codes are important for constructing entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs), but results for non-GRS codes like (L,P)-TGRS codes are limited.
method: The authors analyze a specific class of (L,P)-TGRS codes with a special vector a of length i(q-1), and by considering the parity of i and its relation to q+1, they fully determine the Hermitian hull dimension in three cases.
result: They obtain explicit formulas for the Hermitian hull dimension of these codes and construct two classes of EAQECCs as an application.
conclusion: The work extends the understanding of Hermitian hulls for non-GRS codes and provides new EAQECCs, but the contribution is incremental and the topic is peripheral to the user's core interests.

tldr: This paper studies stable infinite-temperature eigenstates in a SU(2)-symmetric nonintegrable Heisenberg chain, using character theory to count zero-energy states.
motivation: Understanding thermalization in nonintegrable quantum many-body systems is a fundamental problem; the existence of stable eigenstates at infinite temperature challenges the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.
method: The authors consider a bond-staggered Heisenberg chain with spectral reflection symmetry and SU(2) symmetry, employing character theory to count exponentially many zero-energy states and constructing exact low-entangled few-magnon eigenstates.
result: They find exponentially many zero-energy eigenstates that are stable under many perturbations, indicating a violation of thermalization in a nonintegrable model.
conclusion: The existence of such stable eigenstates provides insight into the conditions for thermalization and the role of symmetries in many-body systems.

method: The authors derive a nontrivial multiproduct commutation relation that allows commuting certain sequences of Pauli operators, thereby reducing the number of T gates needed in sequential Pauli-based computation.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which may lead to novel phases and functionalities.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, including dynamical mean-field theory and time-resolved spectroscopy.
result: Identifies key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable states, and nonthermal orders such as superconductivity and magnetism.
conclusion: Photoexcitation in Mott insulators provides a rich platform for exploring nonequilibrium physics and designing new material properties.
