title: The Quantum Harmonic Oscillator In A Dissipative Bath Of Anyon Pairs
authors: A Pelster And M Thorwart N-H Meyer
abstract: We generalize the formalism of open quantum systems to introduce anyon baths. In particular, we work out a dissipative anyon bath composed of independent pairs of one-dimensional Grundberg–Hansson harmonically bound anyons, which are characterized by one statistical parameter. Using a mapping of these anyons to a bosonic bath with rescaled oscillator frequencies, we show that the original bilinear system-bath coupling assumes a particular non-polynomial form. To determine the relaxation properties, we use the imaginary-time path integral formalism together with a generalization of Wick’s theorem in the form of a smearing formula. The latter allows to approximately calculate the anyon bath spectral density, which acquires a nontrivial temperature dependence. The corresponding relaxation dynamics of the dissipative harmonic oscillator in an anyon bath is found. Well defined limits are revealed for both low and high temperatures. Anyonic features turn out to be most pronounced in the regime of intermediate temperatures.
tldr: This paper studies the relaxation dynamics of a quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to a dissipative bath of anyon pairs, using path integral methods and a generalized Wick's theorem.
motivation: To extend open quantum system formalism to anyonic baths, which are of interest in topological quantum computing and fractional statistics.
method: Maps anyon pairs to a bosonic bath with rescaled frequencies, uses imaginary-time path integrals and a smearing formula to approximate the spectral density.
result: The anyon bath spectral density acquires nontrivial temperature dependence; relaxation dynamics show distinct low- and high-temperature limits, with anyonic features most pronounced at intermediate temperatures.
conclusion: The formalism provides a tractable model for anyon baths, but the results are incremental and the connection to core information thermodynamics is weak.

title: Non-equilibrium Coupling To A Diffusing Density Breaks Ising Universality
authors: Mattia Scandolo, Johannes Pausch, Michael E. Cates, Luca Di Carlo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Ising universality class is remarkably robust to non-equilibrium perturbations, which generically flow to zero under renormalization. We show that this robustness fails when an order parameter is coupled nonreciprocally to a conserved diffusive density. Below [MATH], the renormalization group flows to a fast-diffusion fixed point at which the density acts as a long-range multiplicative noise, producing a novel universality class. The non-equilibrium nature of the fixed point is manifest in the large-scale violation of the fluctuation-dissipation relations, reflected in a splitting of the scaling exponents of the two-point correlation and response functions--a measurable hallmark of non-equilibrium critical fluctuations. A two-loop calculation establishes the stability of this fixed point but yields a small correction-to-scaling exponent [MATH] in [MATH], implying strong finite-size corrections. An all-orders modified Harris criterion [MATH] confirms that the BIM fixed point governs criticality in [MATH], with Ising universality recovered only at [MATH].
tldr: This paper shows that coupling an Ising order parameter nonreciprocally to a diffusive density breaks Ising universality, leading to a novel non-equilibrium universality class.
motivation: The Ising universality class is known to be robust to non-equilibrium perturbations, but the authors investigate whether coupling to a conserved diffusive field can overcome this robustness.
method: The authors use renormalization group analysis, including a two-loop calculation, and derive a modified Harris criterion to study the fixed point structure.
result: They find a fast-diffusion fixed point with a new universality class, characterized by violation of fluctuation-dissipation relations and splitting of correlation and response exponents.
conclusion: The non-equilibrium fixed point is stable in d<4, and Ising universality is only recovered at d=4, implying strong finite-size corrections in experiments.

title: Non-equilibrium Phase Transition In The Brownian Ising Model: Field Theory, Renormalization Group, And Exact Results
authors: Luca Di Carlo Mattia Scandolo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a complete field-theoretical renormalization-group (RG) analysis of the Brownian Ising Model (BIM), in which a [MATH] order parameter is coupled to a passive conserved density, breaking detailed balance. Using the Martin-Siggia-Rose formalism and an [MATH] expansion, we show that this density-order parameter coupling is RG-relevant below four dimensions and drives the system to a new non-equilibrium fixed point, distinct from the Ising universality class. Critical exponents are computed at lowest nontrivial order, some of which require a dedicated two-loop analysis. At large scales, the density acts as an effective noise that is white in time but long-range in space, enhancing order-parameter fluctuations and producing a negative anomalous dimension [MATH]. A defining feature of the new class is that the correlation and response functions acquire different anomalous dimensions, [MATH] - a direct, observable signature of fluctuation-dissipation-theorem violation at large scales that cannot occur in equilibrium. We also find a small correction-to-scaling exponent, implying large preasymptotic corrections that must be accounted for in numerical and experimental tests. We further derive a set of relations among renormalization factors that hold to all orders in perturbation theory, following from the linearity of the density dynamics and an emergent shift symmetry. These yield an exact scaling relation [MATH] at the BIM fixed point and establish that the Ising universality class, as well as that of quenched diluted-Ising, is unstable in [MATH]. This establishes the BIM fixed point as the unique infrared attractor for any nonzero diffusion constant.
tldr: This paper studies a non-equilibrium phase transition in the Brownian Ising Model using field theory and renormalization group, identifying a new universality class with violation of fluctuation-dissipation theorem.
motivation: To understand how non-equilibrium conditions, specifically coupling to a conserved density, alter critical behavior compared to equilibrium Ising universality.
method: Martin-Siggia-Rose formalism and epsilon expansion around four dimensions to compute critical exponents and renormalization group flows.
result: The density-order parameter coupling is relevant below four dimensions, leading to a new fixed point with distinct exponents and negative anomalous dimension; correlation and response functions have different anomalous dimensions, signaling fluctuation-dissipation theorem violation.
conclusion: The Brownian Ising Model fixed point is the unique infrared attractor for nonzero diffusion, and the Ising and quenched diluted-Ising classes are unstable in d<4.

title: Second-harmonic Generation From An Optically Levitated Ktp Nanocrystal In Vacuum
authors: Yuanbin Jin, Chenli Gao, Jiayu Feng, Yuxuan Hao, Xudong Yu, Jing Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optically levitated system in vacuum has emerged as a powerful platform for studies of fundamental physics and precision measurements. Although various nanoparticles have been successfully levitated in vacuum, they typically lack the capability to support optical nonlinear processes. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the stable levitation of a potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP) nonlinear nanocrystal in vacuum and investigate its second-harmonic generation (SHG) properties. This levitated system intrinsically provides a pristine dark-background environment with a high signal-to-noise ratio. The trapping laser simultaneously serves as a fundamental light for efficient SHG. Moreover, the polarization of the collected SHG signal is correlated with that of the fundamental laser, providing clear evidence of the optical torque enabling controllable alignment of the nanocrystal with the driving field. Our work establishes a new route toward exploring nonlinear optical processes in vacuum levitation systems and designing novel nanodevices with high manipulation agility in a fully contact-free environment.
tldr: This paper demonstrates second-harmonic generation from an optically levitated KTP nanocrystal in vacuum, focusing on nonlinear optics in a levitated platform.
motivation: Optically levitated nanoparticles in vacuum are useful for fundamental physics and precision measurements, but typically lack nonlinear optical capabilities. The authors aim to introduce nonlinearity by levitating a KTP nanocrystal.
method: A KTP nanocrystal is optically trapped in vacuum using a laser, which simultaneously serves as the fundamental light for second-harmonic generation. The polarization of the SHG signal is analyzed to infer crystal alignment.
result: Stable levitation and efficient SHG are achieved with high signal-to-noise ratio. The polarization correlation between fundamental and SHG light indicates optical torque that aligns the nanocrystal.
conclusion: This work establishes a new route for exploring nonlinear optical processes in vacuum levitation systems and for designing contact-free nanodevices.

title: Heterogeneously Integrated Balanced Photodetector On An Ultra-Low Loss Silicon Nitride Delay Line Interferometer
authors: Rahul Chawlani, Fatemehsadat Tabatabaei, Mark W. Harrington, Kaikai Liu, Steven M. Zhu, Jiawei Wang, Meiting Song, Xiangwen Guo, Andreas Beling, Daniel J. Blumenthal
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thin core silicon nitride photonics enables ultra-low loss, CMOS foundry compatible integration that supports wavelengths from the visible to shortwave infrared. Applications that can benefit from the resulting lower cost, improved robustness, and portability include quantum sensing and computing, ultra-low noise microwave generation, optical clocks, optical gyros, coherent fiber communications, and fiber sensing. An important next step is integration of functional circuits and systems on chip with heterogeneous integration of active components such as high-performance photodetection. Yet to date integrated high-performance photodetectors on the thin film silicon nitride platform has remained elusive. In this work, we demonstrate heterogeneous integration of an InGaAs on InP substrate Modified Uni-Traveling Carrier balanced photodetector with a 15-meter-long unbalanced thin core silicon nitride Mach-Zehnder Interferometer with a bandwidth of 0.92 GHz and a responsivity of 0.305 A/W at 1550 nm with a propagation loss as low as 2.5 dB/m at 1600 nm. Using this circuit we demonstrate two functions, a meter-scale differential interferometer laser stabilization circuit achieving a nearly 23 dB noise suppression at 1 kHz offset and an optical frequency discriminator frequency noise measurement with high sensitivity across 6 orders of magnitude from 10 Hz to 10 MHz. These results demonstrate that the high performance of thin core silicon nitride devices can be combined with integrated high-performance photodetection to realize on-chip stabilized lasers and circuits and pave the path towards full systems on chip.
tldr: Demonstrates heterogeneous integration of a balanced photodetector on a silicon nitride delay line interferometer for laser stabilization and frequency noise measurement.
motivation: To enable on-chip stabilized lasers and full systems on chip by combining ultra-low loss silicon nitride photonics with high-performance photodetection.
method: Heterogeneous integration of an InGaAs/InP modified uni-traveling carrier balanced photodetector with a 15-meter-long unbalanced thin-core silicon nitride Mach-Zehnder interferometer.
result: Achieved 0.92 GHz bandwidth, 0.305 A/W responsivity at 1550 nm, 2.5 dB/m propagation loss, and demonstrated 23 dB noise suppression at 1 kHz offset for laser stabilization.
conclusion: The results pave the path towards full systems on chip for quantum sensing, computing, and other applications.

title: The Binomial Channel: On Capacity, Optimal Inputs, And Beta-Binomial Approximation
authors: Antonino Favano, Mohammadamin Baniasadi, Ian Zieder, Luca Barletta, Alex Dytso
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the binomial channel with input alphabet [MATH] and output alphabet [MATH]. We investigate its capacity and the structure of the capacity-achieving input and output distributions. Since the output alphabet is finite whereas the input alphabet is continuous, different input distributions may induce the same output distribution; hence, uniqueness and support properties of optimal inputs do not follow from strict concavity arguments. We first establish structural properties of the capacity-achieving input distribution. In particular, we show that it is discrete, unique, symmetric around [MATH], and contains the endpoints [MATH] in its support. We also derive location constraints and bounds on the probability masses of support points, and improve the Witsenhausen-type upper bound on the support size from order [MATH] to order [MATH]. We derive explicit nonasymptotic upper and lower bounds on the capacity [MATH]. These bounds imply [MATH] The lower bound is obtained by evaluating the mutual information at the reference input [MATH], which induces a beta-binomial output distribution, while the upper bound follows from a minimax redundancy construction. Finally, we prove an improved lower bound on the support size of the capacity-achieving input distribution. We show that the beta-binomial output induced by [MATH] is asymptotically optimal and close to the capacity-achieving output distribution in relative entropy and [MATH] divergence. We also prove a finite-mixture approximation lower bound showing that the beta-binomial output cannot be approximated too accurately by binomial mixtures with few components. Combining these results yields a support-size lower bound of order [MATH], with explicit constants. Numerical results illustrate the capacity bounds and optimal input distribution.
tldr: This paper studies the capacity and optimal input distributions of the binomial channel, a classical discrete memoryless channel.
motivation: The binomial channel models many practical communication scenarios, and understanding its capacity and optimal inputs is a fundamental problem in classical information theory.
method: The authors use convex optimization, information-theoretic inequalities, and beta-binomial approximations to characterize the capacity-achieving input distribution and derive bounds on capacity and support size.
result: They prove that the optimal input distribution is discrete, symmetric, and includes endpoints, improve support size bounds, and derive nonasymptotic capacity bounds showing the beta-binomial output is asymptotically optimal.
conclusion: The binomial channel's capacity and optimal input structure are now well understood, with tight bounds and asymptotic optimality of a simple reference input.

A double-membrane 3R-MoS

tldr: This paper studies biphoton generation via SPDC in a 3R-MoS2 metasurface, focusing on nonlinear optics and nanophotonics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To enhance spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) photon pair generation using dual-resonant metasurfaces made of 3R-MoS2, a van der Waals material with second-order nonlinearity.
method: Design and simulation of a double-membrane metasurface with two distinct hole arrays supporting high-order multipole resonances, combined with the nonlinear response of 3R-MoS2 to achieve dual-resonant excitation.
result: The metasurface design leads to an increased SPDC photon generation rate compared to an unpatterned flake.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates a viable platform for efficient biphoton sources, but the work is primarily a photonic engineering result without deep quantum information or thermodynamic insights.

title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithms For The Jones Polynomial
authors: Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew Decross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, And Konstantinos Meichanetzidis
abstract:
Author(s): Tuomas Laakkonen, Enrico Rinaldi, Chris N. Self, Eli Chertkov, Matthew DeCross, David Hayes, Brian Neyenhuis, Marcello Benedetti, and Konstantinos Meichanetzidis

A comprehensive quantum algorithmic pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial is shown to serve as a benchmark for quantum computers and yield new insights into potential quantum advantage.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020355] Published Tue Jun 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a complete quantum algorithm pipeline for approximating the Jones polynomial, demonstrating its use as a benchmark for quantum computers.
motivation: The Jones polynomial is a powerful topological invariant that is hard to compute classically, making it a candidate for quantum advantage. The authors aim to provide an end-to-end implementation on current quantum hardware.
method: The algorithm uses a unitary representation of the braid group to encode the Jones polynomial as a quantum amplitude, which is then estimated via Hadamard test and amplitude estimation techniques. The pipeline includes compilation and optimization for trapped-ion quantum processors.
result: Experimental results on a trapped-ion quantum computer show successful approximation of the Jones polynomial for small knots, with error mitigation improving accuracy. The resource requirements scale polynomially with the number of crossings.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical quantum algorithm for a classically hard problem, but the Jones polynomial is not a core focus in the user's research interests, and the paper is more about algorithmic benchmarking than advancing quantum information theory.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: A review of exactly solvable quantum many-body dynamics using space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult; this review aims to provide a unified pedagogical view using space-time duality.
method: The review discusses discretizing time evolution in lattice systems, treating space and time on the same footing, and focuses on brickwork quantum circuits.
result: It presents a unified framework for understanding dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems via space-time duality.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful analogy with quantum computation for solving many-body dynamics.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to analyze neural network activity, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding coordinated activity in large neural networks is a central challenge in neuroscience, and statistical physics offers powerful tools for modeling such systems.
method: The paper reviews maximum entropy models and renormalization group approaches applied to recordings of thousands of neurons, connecting theoretical principles to experimental data.
result: The review highlights that these statistical physics methods uncover reproducible behaviors in neural data, demonstrating predictive power comparable to other areas of physics.
conclusion: Statistical mechanics provides a quantitative bridge between neural data and theoretical principles, advancing our understanding of brain function.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has an irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a global symmetry, which is a topic in quantum information theory but not a core focus.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define subalgebra QCAs, computes topological invariants (anyon permutation and generalized GNVW index), and proves classification results.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: The work provides a classification of symmetric QCAs but is more aligned with quantum cellular automata theory than the researcher's core interests in entanglement, nonlocality, or quantum cryptography.

title: Mlir For Quantum Beyond Gate Cancellation: Quantum Circuit Mapping Reimagined
authors: Matthias Reumann, Yannick Stade, Robert Wille, Lukas Burgholzer
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) framework has become a cornerstone for building extensible, domain-specific compilers, with the quantum computing community already leveraging it to model quantum programs and implement basic optimizations. However, computationally intensive tasks in the quantum compilation pipeline, such as quantum circuit mapping, remain underexplored within the MLIR ecosystem. This paper proposes an MLIR-native blueprint for these non-local, quantum-specific optimization routines by reimplementing a well-established, state-of-the-art mapping A* search algorithm for qubit routing and SWAP insertion. Our evaluation demonstrates that this approach not only integrates seamlessly into an MLIR-based quantum compiler collection but also surpasses previous non-MLIR solutions in both solution quality and runtime. The implementation is open-source and publicly available at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes an MLIR-native implementation of a quantum circuit mapping algorithm, focusing on compiler optimization rather than quantum information theory or physics.
motivation: Quantum circuit mapping is a computationally intensive task in quantum compilation that has not been fully integrated into the MLIR ecosystem.
method: The authors reimplement a state-of-the-art A* search algorithm for qubit routing and SWAP insertion within the MLIR framework.
result: The MLIR-based approach surpasses previous non-MLIR solutions in both solution quality and runtime.
conclusion: MLIR can effectively support non-local quantum optimization routines, enabling seamless integration into quantum compiler collections.

title: Comparing The Performance Of Leading Vqe Algorithms For Computing Ground-State Energies Of Amino Acids
authors: Sanskriti Shindadkar, Clyde Villacrusis, Jasper Andrews, Brandon Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating molecules is a major application of quantum computing, with the potential to overcome exponential scaling constraints of classical computation. Researchers use different methods in order to evaluate the readiness of NISQ computers in order to test current simulation capabilities. We present an integrated repository with reproducible benchmarks of over 10 different ansatzes from published papers and two different truncation methods, applicable to any set of mapped hamiltonians, providing a single pipeline for comparing performance along multiple axes, including variance and computational time, among others. We apply them to simulate different amino acids, using hamiltonians taken from the QMProt Dataset. We then ran four separate experiments. First, we quantified noise resilience by optimizing the same hardware-efficient ansatzes under identical initialization while sweeping PennyLane noise channels and strengths, and measuring parameter drift, cosine similarity of optimal parameters, and energies evaluated on noiseless versus noisy backends. We then studied barren-plateau-related trainability via gradient-variance diagnostics and optimization trajectories across initialization strategies and ansatzes depth on small systems. We then compared adaptive versus fixed ansatzes at matched parameter budgets, reporting outer-loop iterations, wall time, and especially total cost-function evaluations to fairly contrast greedy adaptive growth with layered hardware-efficient circuits. Lastly, we mapped accuracy versus expressive capacity by sweeping the number of retained adaptive operators and recording ground-state energy error relative to classical references.
tldr: This paper benchmarks VQE algorithms for computing ground-state energies of amino acids, focusing on noise resilience, trainability, and accuracy of various ansatzes.
motivation: Simulating molecules is a key application of quantum computing, but NISQ devices face challenges; the paper aims to systematically compare VQE methods to guide algorithm selection.
method: The authors built a repository with over 10 ansatzes and two truncation methods, applied to amino acid Hamiltonians from QMProt. They ran experiments on noise resilience, barren plateau trainability, adaptive vs fixed ansatzes, and accuracy vs expressive capacity.
result: They quantified noise resilience via parameter drift and energy differences, studied gradient variance for trainability, compared adaptive and fixed ansatzes at matched parameter budgets, and mapped accuracy against expressive capacity.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive benchmark for VQE on molecular systems, but the focus is on computational chemistry and algorithm comparison rather than quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Comet: Combinatorial Optimization For Multiplex Editing Targets Via Constraint-Preserving Qaoa
authors: Priyansh Singhal, Sumit Maheshwari, Piyush Joshi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplex CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing requires selecting one guide RNA per target gene subject to cross-gene interactions: a constrained combinatorial problem that can be formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) and solved via the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). The one-hot per-gene constraint is conventionally enforced by adding quadratic penalty terms to the cost Hamiltonian, but penalty coefficient selection is heuristic and penalties amplify hardware noise. An alternative is to enforce the constraint structurally via the XY-mixer, which preserves feasibility by construction. We present COMET, a systematic comparison of penalty-based and XY-mixer QAOA on a three-gene, twelve-qubit multiplex editing instance targeting the immune-checkpoint genes PDCD1, LAG3, and HAVCR2. In simulation, the XY-mixer exceeds 95% probability of the optimum by QAOA depth p=3, while three penalty variants spanning an order of magnitude in penalty coefficient remain below 6% at every depth. On IBM's ibm_kingston (Heron r2) processor, the XY-mixer's simulator-hardware energy gap stays within |0.8| across all depths, while the worst-tuned penalty variant's gap reaches +53.9. We provide an honest account of where the structural guarantee partially breaks under gate-level noise. The twelve-qubit instance is classically trivial; our contribution is a methodological comparison of constraint-enforcement strategies in a biologically motivated domain, with real-hardware validation.
tldr: This paper compares penalty-based and XY-mixer QAOA for a multiplex CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing combinatorial optimization problem, finding the XY-mixer significantly outperforms penalty methods in simulation and on IBM hardware.
motivation: Multiplex CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing requires selecting guide RNAs under cross-gene constraints, a combinatorial problem that can be solved via QAOA. The conventional penalty-based constraint enforcement suffers from heuristic coefficient selection and noise amplification, motivating a structural constraint approach using the XY-mixer.
method: The authors formulate the problem as a QUBO and compare three penalty-based QAOA variants (with different penalty coefficients) against an XY-mixer QAOA that enforces the one-hot constraint structurally. They simulate all variants and run them on IBM's ibm_kingston processor for a three-gene, twelve-qubit instance.
result: In simulation, the XY-mixer achieves >95% probability of the optimum by depth p=3, while penalty variants remain below 6%. On hardware, the XY-mixer's energy gap stays within |0.8|, whereas the worst penalty variant's gap reaches +53.9.
conclusion: The XY-mixer provides a robust constraint enforcement strategy for QAOA on this biologically motivated problem, though the structural guarantee partially breaks under gate-level noise. The instance is classically trivial, so the contribution is methodological.

title: An Approach For Calculating Astrophysical Opacities On Quantum Computers
authors: Shivesh Pathak, Alina Kononov, Andrew D. Baczewski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a quantum algorithmic protocol for calculating astrophysical opacities. Our implementation uses first- and second-quantized representations of interacting electronic and photonic subsystems and Hamiltonian simulation via the interaction picture. Inferring opacity from momentum-resolved measurements of the photonic register yields a direct relationship between qubit count and spectral range/resolution. Logical resource estimates for the classically challenging problem of solar iron opacity are comparable to another high-energy-density physics problem (Rubin et al., PNAS 121(3) (2024)).
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm for calculating astrophysical opacities, which is an application of quantum computing to a classical physics problem.
motivation: Astrophysical opacities are computationally challenging for classical computers, especially for iron in the solar interior. The authors aim to leverage quantum computing to solve this problem.
method: The protocol uses first- and second-quantized representations of interacting electronic and photonic subsystems, Hamiltonian simulation via the interaction picture, and momentum-resolved measurements of the photonic register to infer opacity.
result: Logical resource estimates for solar iron opacity are comparable to another high-energy-density physics problem, suggesting feasibility.
conclusion: Quantum computers may offer a path to calculating opacities that are classically intractable, but the work is a proposal with resource estimates, not an experimental demonstration.

title: Robust Phase Sensitivity In Mach-Zehnder Interferometer Using Photon Added And Subtracted Squeezed Coherent State
authors: Shivani Singh, Priya Malpani, Anirban Pathak
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the precision-based measurements, Mach-Zehnder interferometry is a widely used technique. There are various ways to enhance the precision of Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI), e.g., having a non-classical input state is one of the ways to enhance the precision of the phase estimation performed by MZI. The phase estimation performed by MZI is investigated here by considering that the input states of MZI are different combinations of photon added and subtracted squeezed coherent states (PASCS and PSSCS). Using quantum Fisher information, it is shown that the use of PASCS in both the input modes of MZI, provides the most precise estimate of the unknown phase. This system is also analyzed in two different measurement scenarios -- single intensity detection (SID) and intensity difference detection (IDD). Systematic analysis has established that the intensity measurement might not be an optimal measurement scheme for phase estimation in MZI as phase and intensity correspond to non-commuting observables. The impact of the photon loss on the MZI-based phase estimation setup is also studied and it is found that PASCS is robust against photon loss, when the loss in MZI is low.
tldr: This paper studies phase sensitivity enhancement in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer using photon-added and subtracted squeezed coherent states, analyzing quantum Fisher information and measurement schemes.
motivation: To improve the precision of phase estimation in interferometry by using non-classical input states.
method: The authors consider different combinations of photon-added and subtracted squeezed coherent states as inputs to a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, compute quantum Fisher information, and analyze single intensity detection and intensity difference detection schemes.
result: Photon-added squeezed coherent states provide the most precise phase estimate and are robust against low photon loss.
conclusion: Photon-added squeezed coherent states are a promising resource for robust phase estimation in interferometry.

title: Fringe Field Induced spin-OAM Mixing Of Twisted Electrons
authors: S. S. Baturin S. V. Gatalina
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study spin effects in twisted-electron propagation through the entrance or exit region of an axially symmetric magnetic coil. Starting from the Foldy-Wouthuysen reduction of the Dirac equation, we derive a paraxial spinor equation in which the longitudinally varying solenoidal field produces, in addition to the usual diagonal Zeeman term, a transverse Pauli coupling proportional to the fringe-field gradient. The scalar transverse dynamics is treated exactly by the Ermakov mapping, which absorbs the longitudinally dependent focusing into a metaplectic scaling transformation and reduces the orbital evolution to that of a stationary two-dimensional oscillator. On this background, the transverse Pauli term is treated perturbatively and yields an explicit first-order correction for arbitrary realistic solenoidal profiles. Axial symmetry implies conservation of the total projection of angular momentum, so each spin flip is accompanied by a compensating one-quantum change of orbital angular momentum. In addition, the linear coordinate structure of the perturbation restricts the first-order dynamics to at most two neighboring radial sidebands for each incoming oscillator component. We derive the corresponding transition amplitudes and show how their phases are governed jointly by the Ermakov accumulation and the diagonal spin-orbital rotation. The resulting framework provides a direct way to quantify spin-orbit mixing of twisted electrons in realistic magnetic lenses and solenoidal beam-line elements, and it identifies a route toward controlled spin-OAM conversion in engineered sequences of magnetic-field edges.
tldr: This paper studies spin-orbit mixing of twisted electrons in magnetic fringe fields, deriving transition amplitudes for spin-OAM conversion.
motivation: To understand and quantify spin-orbit coupling effects in twisted electron beams passing through realistic magnetic lenses, which is relevant for electron microscopy and beam manipulation.
method: Starting from the Foldy-Wouthuysen reduction of the Dirac equation, a paraxial spinor equation is derived. The scalar transverse dynamics is solved exactly via Ermakov mapping, and the transverse Pauli term is treated perturbatively to obtain first-order corrections.
result: Axial symmetry conserves total angular momentum, so each spin flip is accompanied by a one-quantum change in orbital angular momentum. Transition amplitudes are derived, showing how phases depend on Ermakov accumulation and spin-orbital rotation.
conclusion: The framework provides a way to quantify spin-orbit mixing of twisted electrons in magnetic lenses and suggests routes for controlled spin-OAM conversion.

title: Single-acquisition Tomography Of Photonic Qubits With Structured Media
authors: Francesco Di Colandrea, Yingwen Zhang, John Grace, Dilip Paneru, Alessio D'errico, Ebrahim Karimi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography is an essential tool for characterizing quantum systems and underpins nearly every experimental realization of quantum technologies. Conventional tomography relies on performing a sequence of projective measurements on many identical copies of a quantum state, requiring the measurement apparatus to be reconfigured between successive acquisitions. As the Hilbert-space dimension increases, the number of required measurements grows rapidly; in practice, additional overcomplete measurements are often performed to improve robustness to experimental imperfections. Here, we introduce a tomography platform based on structured anisotropic media that performs informationally complete measurements of photonic polarization qubits within a single acquisition. The approach employs three liquid-crystal metasurfaces with spatially varying optic-axis orientations that transform the input polarization into a far-field distribution of discrete transverse-momentum modes. Each diffraction pattern uniquely determines the polarization state, enabling its reconstruction without sequential changes to the measurement apparatus. Unlike previous implementations, our scheme is intrinsically photon-number independent: the same optical device operates identically for arbitrary photon numbers, while the desired photon-number sector can be selected afterwards through post-selection of the corresponding [MATH]-fold coincidence events. We experimentally demonstrate single-frame quantum state tomography of both single- and two-photon polarization states, providing a simple and scalable route toward efficient quantum-state characterization.
tldr: A tomography platform using structured anisotropic media for single-acquisition quantum state tomography of photonic polarization qubits.
motivation: Conventional quantum state tomography requires many projective measurements and reconfiguration, which is inefficient for high-dimensional states. The authors aim to develop a faster, single-shot method.
method: Three liquid-crystal metasurfaces with spatially varying optic-axis orientations transform input polarization into a far-field diffraction pattern, enabling informationally complete measurements without sequential changes.
result: Experimental demonstration of single-frame tomography for single- and two-photon polarization states, with the scheme being photon-number independent.
conclusion: The approach provides a simple and scalable route toward efficient quantum-state characterization, reducing measurement time and complexity.

title: Orbit-q: Dual-axis Benchmarking Of Autonomous Agents In Scientific Quantum Programming
authors: Yu-Qin Chen Shi-Xin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous coding agents perform well on many conventional programming tasks, but scientific computing demands a rigorous validation paradigm that extends beyond simple functional test completion: generated code must preserve physical fidelity, differentiable workflows, framework-native semantics, and scalable representations. We introduce Open Research Benchmark for Integrated Tasks in Quantum Computing (ORBIT-Q) to address this gap. At its core, ORBIT-Q contributes a carefully curated suite of complex, research-level quantum workflows that serves as a challenging testbed for modern scientific programming. ORBIT-Q combines a rigorous multi-tier verification pipeline to support two orthogonal comparisons: different agent harness and model configurations at a fixed quantum software framework, and different quantum software frameworks at a fixed agent. In our systematic evaluations, TensorCircuit-NG (TC) exhibits the highest capability and performance efficiency among the evaluated quantum software frameworks under agent-driven programming, and Codex with GPT-5.5 is the strongest tested agent configuration on TC. However, a significant performance and design gap remains between frontier autonomous agents and human expert reference implementations. We further evaluate two efficiency dimensions: agent-side resource use and artifact-side runtime. Together, these results establish ORBIT-Q as a rigorous benchmark for autonomous scientific programming, framework-agent synergy, and quantum software performance.
tldr: This paper introduces ORBIT-Q, a benchmark for evaluating autonomous coding agents in scientific quantum programming, focusing on framework-agent synergy and code fidelity.
motivation: Existing benchmarks for autonomous coding agents lack rigorous validation for scientific computing, especially in quantum programming where physical fidelity and differentiable workflows are critical.
method: ORBIT-Q provides a curated suite of research-level quantum workflows and a multi-tier verification pipeline to compare agent harnesses and quantum software frameworks.
result: TensorCircuit-NG and Codex with GPT-5.5 performed best, but a significant gap remains between autonomous agents and human expert implementations.
conclusion: ORBIT-Q establishes a rigorous benchmark for autonomous scientific programming and highlights the need for further improvement in agent-driven quantum software development.

title: Operator-theoretic Approach To The Partial Integration Of Randomly Coupled Phase Oscillators
authors: Vincent Thibeault, Benjamin Claveau, Antoine Allard, Patrick Desrosiers
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In our previous work [arXiv:2504.06248], we adopted Koopman theory to link the existence of different constants of motion to the presence of specific network motifs of Kuramoto oscillators. Yet, it remains to be shown how the partial integration can be carried out using the Koopman generator and its eigenfunctions. In this paper, we construct a random graph from network motifs that admit Koopman eigenfunctions and conserved quantities, and use it to define a partially integrable Kuramoto model. We perform the partial integration of the introduced model when there are monomial eigenfunctions and conserved cross-ratios, while providing an operator-theoretic derivation of the Watanabe-Strogatz transformation based on Magnus expansion and a recent result on closed forms of the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula [arXiv:1502.06589].
tldr: This paper uses Koopman operator theory to analyze partial integrability in randomly coupled Kuramoto phase oscillators.
motivation: The authors aim to extend their previous work on Koopman theory and network motifs to explicitly perform partial integration of Kuramoto models.
method: They construct a random graph from network motifs that admit Koopman eigenfunctions and conserved quantities, then derive a partially integrable Kuramoto model using operator-theoretic techniques including Magnus expansion and Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula.
result: They achieve partial integration of the model with monomial eigenfunctions and conserved cross-ratios, providing an operator-theoretic derivation of the Watanabe-Strogatz transformation.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a novel operator-theoretic approach to partial integration in coupled oscillator networks, but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Physics-Informed Tensor Completion With Application To Distribution System State Estimation
authors: Alexander While, Anil Aswani, Chen Chen, William N. Caballero
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State estimation in power distribution networks often involves sparse, noisy, and heterogeneous measurements, making classical weighted least-squares methods unreliable in low-observability regimes. To meet this challenge we develop a physics-informed low-rank tensor completion method. The method encodes voltage phasor components, voltage magnitudes, and power injections over time in a low-rank tensor, while incorporating physics through convex residual penalties. For distribution network state estimation, these residuals are instantiated using linearized power-flow equations, yielding a convex optimization problem over a tensor gauge ball, equivalently represented as a polytope implicitly described via integer programming. We solve this problem using globally convergent blended conditional gradients, resulting in a general-purpose algorithmic framework that can be adapted across different domains and applications where low-rank structure and convex physics residuals are available. We also derive a deterministic error bound showing that, under a restricted stability condition, the estimation error is controlled by measurement noise and physics-model mismatch. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method substantially improves state recovery compared with purely data-driven tensor completion and weighted least-squares, especially in low-observability regimes with missing data.
tldr: This paper applies tensor completion with physics-informed constraints to power distribution system state estimation.
motivation: Classical state estimation methods fail in low-observability regimes with sparse, noisy measurements; a new method is needed.
method: A low-rank tensor completion method is developed that encodes voltage and power data while incorporating linearized power-flow equations as convex residual penalties, solved via blended conditional gradients.
result: The method substantially improves state recovery over purely data-driven tensor completion and weighted least-squares, especially with missing data.
conclusion: Physics-informed tensor completion is effective for distribution system state estimation and can be adapted to other domains with low-rank structure and convex physics residuals.

title: Open Problem: Is Interaction Necessary For Order-Optimal 1-bit Mean Estimation?
authors: Jonathan Scarlett Ivan Lau
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask whether interaction is necessary for order-optimal 1-bit mean estimation over nonparametric finite-moment classes. Adaptive threshold-query protocols achieve the order-optimal 1-bit minimax rate, and the same rate is attainable with general 1-bit queries using only one adaptive transition (i.e., two stages of querying). In the non-adaptive setting, threshold and interval queries are known to be highly suboptimal, but the case of arbitrary non-adaptive quantizers remains unresolved. Can such quantizers match the adaptive rate, yielding an optimal one-shot protocol? Or is the known two-stage estimator stage-optimal, with a single adaptive transition being necessary and sufficient?
tldr: This paper asks whether interaction is necessary for order-optimal 1-bit mean estimation over nonparametric finite-moment classes.
motivation: Understanding the role of interaction in statistical estimation is a fundamental question in learning theory.
method: The paper compares adaptive and non-adaptive query protocols for 1-bit mean estimation, analyzing minimax rates.
result: Adaptive threshold-query protocols achieve order-optimal rates, and the same rate is attainable with two stages of querying; non-adaptive threshold and interval queries are suboptimal, but the case of arbitrary non-adaptive quantizers remains open.
conclusion: The paper poses an open problem: whether non-adaptive arbitrary quantizers can match the adaptive rate, or if a single adaptive transition is necessary and sufficient.

title: Gevrey Regularity And Compact Quantum Metric Spaces For $L^p$-Group Algebras
authors: Qin Wang Lin Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the beta-Gevrey lp-rapid decay property (GRD){beta,p}, for 0 < beta <= 1 and 1 <= p < infinity, for countable discrete groups. This property is a subexponential analogue of classical rapid decay, in which polynomial control is replaced by logarithmic subexponential control of order o(R^beta). We establish basic results for (GRD){beta,p}. We then apply this framework to compact quantum metric structures on reduced Lp-group algebras. We introduce strongly dense-core beta-Gevrey regular lp-spectral triples and give two classes of examples. For countable discrete groups satisfying (GRD)_{beta,p}, we prove, using Rieffel's criterion, that the corresponding Gevrey seminorms induce metrics on the Banach-algebra state space which metrize the weak-* topology. This yields compact quantum metric space structures in settings beyond classical rapid decay, including groups of intermediate growth such as the first Grigorchuk group.
tldr: This paper introduces Gevrey regularity for Lp-group algebras and constructs compact quantum metric spaces, but does not align with the user's research directions.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the concept of rapid decay to subexponential control and apply it to compact quantum metric structures on reduced Lp-group algebras.
method: They define the beta-Gevrey lp-rapid decay property for discrete groups and use Rieffel's criterion to show that Gevrey seminorms induce metrics on state spaces.
result: They prove that for groups satisfying (GRD)_{beta,p}, the Gevrey seminorms metrize the weak-* topology, yielding compact quantum metric space structures beyond classical rapid decay.
conclusion: The work provides new examples of compact quantum metric spaces, including groups of intermediate growth like the first Grigorchuk group.

title: Entropy Regularization Improves Policy Robustness In Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jialun Cao, Fernando Acero, David \v{s}i\v{s}ka, Yufei Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entropy regularization is widely used in continuous-time reinforcement learning (RL) to reduce sensitivity to environmental perturbations, yet its robustness benefits lack a rigorous theoretical foundation. This paper establishes the first robustness guarantees for entropy-regularized continuous-time Markov decision processes. We show that maximizing an entropy-regularized objective yields a lower bound on a worst-case robust RL problem with joint reward and transition perturbations. We analytically characterize the induced robust sets and prove that they expand monotonically with the regularization strength, justifying the empirical observation that stronger entropy improves robustness. In contrast to prior discrete-time analyses, our results remove the intractable state-distribution entropy term and provide guarantees invariant to action frequency. Experiments on queueing network control and market making confirm our theory, showing that entropy-regularized policies outperform greedy and [MATH]-greedy baselines under dynamics perturbations.
tldr: This paper establishes robustness guarantees for entropy-regularized continuous-time reinforcement learning, showing that entropy regularization improves policy robustness against environmental perturbations.
motivation: Entropy regularization is empirically known to improve robustness in RL, but lacks rigorous theoretical foundations, especially in continuous-time settings.
method: The authors prove that maximizing an entropy-regularized objective yields a lower bound on a worst-case robust RL problem with joint reward and transition perturbations, and characterize the induced robust sets.
result: They show that robust sets expand monotonically with regularization strength, and their guarantees remove the intractable state-distribution entropy term present in discrete-time analyses.
conclusion: Entropy-regularized policies outperform greedy and epsilon-greedy baselines under dynamics perturbations, as confirmed by experiments on queueing network control and market making.

title: Diffusion-Based Noise-Adaptive Null-Space Channel Estimation For Ofdm Systems
authors: Heqiang Qi, Yirun Chen, Xiangming Meng, Chunxiao Jiang, Sheng Wu, Linling Kuang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate channel estimation in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems remains challenging when demodulation reference signal (DMRS) observations are sparse and noisy, and when DMRS configurations vary across deployment scenarios. This paper proposes DANCE (Diffusion-based Noise-Adaptive Null-space Channel Estimation), a diffusion-based channel estimator for OFDM systems. We formulate DMRS-aided channel estimation as a sparse linear inverse problem whose measurement operator is induced by the pilot pattern. The resulting range-null space decomposition separates the measurement-constrained range-space component from the unobserved null-space component, which is reconstructed through a learned diffusion prior. To avoid directly imposing noisy pilot samples as exact constraints, DANCE introduces a noise-adaptive posterior correction into the reverse diffusion process. The correction coefficient and the residual sampling variance are jointly calibrated according to the observation noise level, thereby reducing pilot-noise injection while retaining useful measurement information. We further design a conditional U-Net denoiser for complex-valued OFDM channel grids, where the real and imaginary components are represented as separate feature channels and downsampling is performed only along the subcarrier dimension. Simulations based on 5G NR tapped delay line (TDL) and clustered delay line (CDL) channel models show that DANCE achieves consistently lower normalized mean squared error (NMSE) than conventional estimators and diffusion-based posterior sampling methods under different signal-to-noise ratios, DMRS configurations, Doppler frequency shifts, and train-test distribution mismatches.
tldr: This paper proposes a diffusion-based channel estimation method for OFDM systems using noise-adaptive null-space reconstruction.
motivation: Accurate channel estimation in OFDM systems is challenging when DMRS observations are sparse and noisy, and configurations vary across deployment scenarios.
method: DANCE formulates DMRS-aided channel estimation as a sparse linear inverse problem, separates range and null spaces, and uses a diffusion prior with noise-adaptive posterior correction to reconstruct the null-space component.
result: Simulations on 5G NR channel models show that DANCE achieves consistently lower NMSE than conventional estimators and other diffusion-based methods under various conditions.
conclusion: The proposed method improves channel estimation accuracy and robustness, but the work is focused on classical wireless communications without quantum information or thermodynamics aspects.

title: Minimax Estimation Of Kernel Stein Discrepancy: Trace Versus Hilbert-Schmidt Scales
authors: Davit Gogolashvili
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel Stein Discrepancy (KSD) compares a sample to a fixed target distribution known only through its score, and is widely used for goodness-of-fit testing, sample quality assessment, and approximate inference. We study the estimation of [MATH] from [MATH] independent observations and identify the sharp spectral constant governing the minimax risk: it is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the Stein covariance operator [MATH], giving the minimax scale [MATH]. This scale is attained by the positive-part square-root U-statistic, whereas the standard plug-in V-statistic remains at the trace scale [MATH] and is therefore suboptimal by the fourth root of the effective rank of [MATH]; for a Gaussian target with a fixed-bandwidth Gaussian kernel this factor is exponential in the dimension.
tldr: This paper studies minimax estimation of kernel Stein discrepancy, identifying optimal convergence rates in terms of Hilbert-Schmidt vs trace norms.
motivation: Kernel Stein discrepancy is used for goodness-of-fit testing and sample quality assessment, but its estimation risk and optimal rates were not fully understood.
method: The authors derive sharp spectral constants and compare the performance of U-statistics and V-statistics for estimating KSD.
result: The minimax optimal rate is governed by the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the Stein covariance operator, and the positive-part square-root U-statistic achieves it, while the plug-in V-statistic is suboptimal.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guidance for choosing estimators in KSD-based applications, but is purely statistical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Sketch Low-rank Dynamics: Orthogonal Vs. Oblique Projections
authors: Laura Grigori Benjamin Carrel
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how sketching techniques from randomized numerical linear algebra can be incorporated into the dynamical low-rank approximation (DLRA) of large-scale matrix differential equations. A natural approach is to sketch the Galerkin condition that defines the DLRA, which leads to an oblique tangent space projection. We show that this oblique projection approximately reproduces the standard DLRA only under restrictive conditions on the vector field, and that it fails on problems with a large perpendicular residual. As an alternative, we propose an orthogonal sketch DLRA that evolves sketch-orthogonal bases while using standard orthogonal projections for the dynamics. This approach preserves the geometric structure of the classical DLRA and is numerically stable. The computational advantage of randomized Gram--Schmidt over Householder QR lies in fewer global synchronizations on a row-distributed basis, at a comparable flop count; when the basis is well conditioned, randomized Gram--Schmidt can be replaced by randomized Cholesky QR, which additionally shifts the basis update from BLAS-2 to BLAS-3 kernels, making it well-suited to modern accelerators. We derive sketch versions of the projector-splitting and BUG integrators, and demonstrate the approach on the Allen--Cahn, Fokker--Planck, and Vlasov--Poisson equations.
tldr: This paper studies sketching techniques for dynamical low-rank approximation of matrix differential equations, focusing on orthogonal vs oblique projections.
motivation: To improve computational efficiency of dynamical low-rank approximation for large-scale matrix differential equations using randomized numerical linear algebra.
method: Compares oblique projection (sketched Galerkin condition) with orthogonal sketch DLRA that evolves sketch-orthogonal bases using standard orthogonal projections; derives sketch versions of projector-splitting and BUG integrators.
result: Oblique projection fails on problems with large perpendicular residual; orthogonal sketch DLRA preserves geometric structure and is numerically stable, with computational advantages in synchronization and BLAS operations.
conclusion: Orthogonal sketch DLRA is a viable and efficient approach for large-scale matrix differential equations, particularly suited to modern accelerators.

title: Scalable Differentially Private Data Compression Via Diffusion And Stochastic Codes
authors: Gergely Flamich, Oyk\"u S{\i}la G\"uner, Yanxiao Liu, Deniz G\"und\"uz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ever-increasing collection of personal data has created mounting pressure to develop technologies that protect sensitive aspects of individual identity. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled framework with strong formal guarantees and has already achieved practical success. However, releasing high-dimensional data, such as images, has remained elusive: releasing uncompressed privatized data requires significant storage. At the same time, no effective data compression scheme exists that can compress high-resolution data with privacy guarantees. We address this challenge with DP-DiPP, a compression pipeline that combines stochastic codes with diffusion models. DP-DiPP is highly flexible: the practitioner has direct control over the compression rate-privacy-utility tradeoff. As the theoretical backbone, we extend the Poisson private representation (PPR) to encode the outputs of privacy mechanisms. We then combine it with DiffC, a diffusion-based lossy data compression method, to obtain a differentially private image compressor. Our experiments on privatized image classification on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that DP-DiPP significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10-30 times better compression while retaining comparable privacy guarantees and utility.
tldr: This paper proposes a differentially private image compression pipeline using stochastic codes and diffusion models.
motivation: Releasing high-dimensional private data like images requires both privacy guarantees and efficient compression, which existing methods lack.
method: The authors extend Poisson private representation (PPR) to encode outputs of privacy mechanisms and combine it with a diffusion-based lossy compression method (DiffC) to create DP-DiPP.
result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 show DP-DiPP achieves 10-30 times better compression than baselines while maintaining comparable privacy and utility.
conclusion: DP-DiPP offers a flexible tradeoff between compression rate, privacy, and utility for high-dimensional data.

title: The Informational Cost Of Structure: Representational Complexity In Networked Dynamical Systems
authors: Cyril Rommens, Pietro Traversa, Guilherme Ferraz de Arruda, Yamir Moreno
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information is required to represent a dynamical system in terms of an interaction structure and an evolution rule? We address this question using algorithmic information theory. We introduce Representational Complexity, the excess description length of a structure-plus-rule model relative to the shortest possible description of the dynamics itself. This intrinsic description defines a universal lower bound: no exact structural representation can be more concise. If arbitrary rules are allowed, graphs, hypergraphs, and other formalisms can all reach this bound by shifting information between structure and dynamics, so expressiveness alone cannot distinguish them. Meaningful differences arise only when scientific modeling restricts the admissible structures and rules. Within this setting, we identify conditions under which graph and hypergraph descriptions are informationally equivalent, and show how graph-preferred, hypergraph-preferred, and mixed regimes can emerge when those conditions are relaxed. Because Kolmogorov complexity is not computable, we complement the formal results with explicit description-length estimates. Our framework reframes the choice of network representation as a question of informational cost and mechanistic transparency rather than universal expressive power.
tldr: This paper uses algorithmic information theory to analyze the representational cost of modeling dynamical systems with network structures.
motivation: To understand how much information is needed to represent a dynamical system in terms of an interaction structure and evolution rule, and to compare different network formalisms.
method: Introduces Representational Complexity based on Kolmogorov complexity, and provides formal conditions for informational equivalence between graph and hypergraph descriptions.
result: Graphs, hypergraphs, and other formalisms can all achieve the universal lower bound by shifting information between structure and dynamics; meaningful differences arise only under restricted modeling assumptions.
conclusion: The choice of network representation should be guided by informational cost and mechanistic transparency rather than universal expressive power.

title: Observer-Quotient Security: Composable Leakage Bounds For Hidden State Continuations
authors: Levent Sarioglu Faruk Alpay
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observer-quotient security studies interactive cryptographic systems whose security depends on what an admissible observer can distinguish across transcripts, leakage traces, and hidden implementation continuations. The paper defines observer-indexed experiments with session identifiers, adaptive schedulers, oracle forwarding, simulators, ideal quotient functionalities, and nonuniform environments, and proves a real/ideal emulation theorem in which sequential morphism defects add, parallel defects obey a product-TV bound, and adaptive observer choice is absorbed by an explicit wrapper construction. The resulting advantage bound is indexed by [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and the residual floor [MATH]. The framework is instantiated for IND-CPA encryption with timing leakage, deterministic encryption with entropy ledgers, and finite-state side-channel refinement under transcript, timing, cache, power, EM, and profiled observers. The optimization/control component identifies hidden continuations with observability kernels, treats sensor redesign as quotient refinement, and converts dissipativity, PL-type rates, and ISS residual bounds into concrete reductions in distinguishing advantage. Ancillary code and synthetic data reproduce the finite-state leakage audit and LTI observer-design benchmark.
tldr: The paper introduces observer-quotient security, a framework for composable leakage bounds in cryptographic systems with hidden state continuations.
motivation: To provide a rigorous security model that accounts for side-channel leakage and adaptive observers in interactive cryptographic protocols.
method: Defines observer-indexed experiments with session identifiers, adaptive schedulers, and simulators, proving a real/ideal emulation theorem with sequential and parallel composition bounds.
result: Derives advantage bounds indexed by multiple parameters and instantiates the framework for IND-CPA encryption with timing leakage and finite-state side-channel refinement.
conclusion: The framework offers composable security guarantees against various side-channel observers, with applications to leakage auditing and sensor redesign.

title: Function-Correcting Codes For Sum-Rank Metric
authors: B. Sundar Rajan Santhi Kumari Kammila
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Function-Correcting Codes (FCCs) are a class of codes designed to protect the evaluation of a specific function of a message against channel errors at a higher level than the level of protection for the message, while requiring significantly less redundancy than conventional error-correcting codes. In this paper, we study function-correcting codes under the sum-rank metric, which is a natural generalization of both the Hamming metric and the rank-metric and also we derive general upper and lower bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs in the sum-rank metric. In particular, we establish a Plotkin-like bound for irregular-distance codes in sum-rank metric. Furthermore, we present explicit construction of function-correcting sum-rank metric codes (FCSRCs) for locally binary functions with optimal redundancy.
tldr: This paper studies function-correcting codes under the sum-rank metric, deriving bounds and constructions.
motivation: To protect function evaluations of messages against channel errors with less redundancy than conventional error-correcting codes.
method: Generalizes function-correcting codes to the sum-rank metric, establishes a Plotkin-like bound for irregular-distance codes, and provides explicit constructions for locally binary functions.
result: Derives general upper and lower bounds on optimal redundancy and presents optimal constructions for locally binary functions.
conclusion: Function-correcting codes in the sum-rank metric can achieve significant redundancy savings for protecting specific functions.
