motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but most known flat bands require cryogenic temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature stable platform.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and characterize their electronic structure using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and density functional theory (DFT).
result: They observe intrinsic flat bands that are orbital-selective and remain stable at room temperature, with tunability via material composition.
conclusion: These materials provide a promising platform for studying strongly correlated electron physics at room temperature, potentially enabling practical applications.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall States In Twisted Bilayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ Via Attractive Polaron Spectroscopy
authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi
abstract:
Author(s): Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, and Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021037] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted bilayer WSe2, revealing a quantum anomalous Hall phase and electric-field control of magnetic order.
motivation: To investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of twisted bilayer WSe2, a moiré material, and to demonstrate control over its quantum anomalous Hall state.
method: Magneto-optical spectroscopy, specifically attractive polaron spectroscopy, is used to probe the electronic structure and magnetic phases under varying electric and magnetic fields.
result: A spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase is observed, and electric-field control enables transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the physics of twisted bilayer WSe2 and demonstrates a platform for exploring topological phases and magnetic order in moiré systems.

title: Liquid-Gas Criticality Of Hyperuniform Fluids
authors: Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, And Qun-Li Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, and Qun-Li Lei

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021032] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, a topic in soft condensed matter physics with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Hyperuniform fluids exhibit suppressed density fluctuations, and their critical behavior at the liquid-vapor transition is of fundamental interest in statistical mechanics.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling and possibly simulations to analyze the critical properties of hyperuniform fluids composed of spinning particles.
result: They find that hyperuniform fluids remain unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid-vapor critical point, contrasting with ordinary fluids.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the critical behavior of hyperuniform systems, but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in stealthy hyperuniform photonic crystals, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show residual scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale experiments on silicon photonic crystals combined with theoretical analysis to characterize the scattering behavior.
result: Residual scattering is driven by radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of full transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight limitations of stealthy hyperuniformity for photonic applications and suggest design modifications.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates a dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, focusing on the structural and dielectric properties of these materials.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex behavior that is not fully understood; understanding the nematic ordering may help explain their unique properties.
method: The authors use experimental techniques and theoretical modeling to characterize the dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics.
result: They identify a dipolar nematic phase and describe its impact on the material's dielectric response.
conclusion: The dipolar nematic state is a key feature of relaxor ferroelectrics, and its study advances the understanding of these materials.

title: Breakdown Of The Thermodynamic Limit In Quantum Spin And Dimer Models
authors: Jeet Shah, Laura Shou, Jeremy Shuler, And Victor Galitski
abstract:
Author(s): Jeet Shah, Laura Shou, Jeremy Shuler, and Victor Galitski

Geometry-induced quantum phase separation in quantum dimer models demonstrates that domain shape can fundamentally alter macroscopic ground states, challenging traditional assumptions about the thermodynamic limit.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021020] Published Mon Apr 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that domain shape can fundamentally alter macroscopic ground states in quantum dimer models, challenging the thermodynamic limit.
motivation: To investigate whether the thermodynamic limit assumption holds in quantum spin and dimer models with geometry-induced phase separation.
method: The authors study quantum dimer models on lattices with specific domain shapes and analyze ground state properties using analytical and numerical methods.
result: They find that the shape of the domain can lead to different macroscopic ground states, indicating a breakdown of the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: Geometry-induced quantum phase separation can invalidate the thermodynamic limit in certain quantum spin and dimer models.

title: Excitations Across The Equilibrium And Photoinduced “Hidden” States Of Magnetoresistive Manganites
authors: Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, And Jonathan Pelliciari
abstract:
Author(s): Shiyu Fan, Feng Jin, Taehun Kim, Umesh Kumar, Zixun Zhang, Vivek Bhartiya, Jiemin Li, Brandon Yalin, Yanhong Gu, Mingqiang Gu, Wen Hu, Claudio Mazzoli, G. Lawrence Carr, Osor S. Barišić, Andrey S. Mishchenko, Valentina Bisogni, Sobhit Singh, Wenbin Wu, and Jonathan Pelliciari

Ultrafast photoexcitation in /3Ca1/3MnO3 generates a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations that do not exist under standard equilibrium conditions.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021018] Published Thu Apr 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies photoinduced hidden phases in magnetoresistive manganites using ultrafast spectroscopy.
motivation: To understand the non-equilibrium dynamics and hidden phases in strongly correlated electron systems.
method: Ultrafast photoexcitation and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to probe excitations.
result: Discovery of a long-lived hidden phase with unique polaronic and phononic excitations not present in equilibrium.
conclusion: Photoexcitation can induce metastable states with distinct properties in manganites.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis is proposed, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a classical machine learning technique; quantum speedups could enable analysis of larger datasets.
method: The paper designs a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and topological invariants to compute persistence diagrams.
result: The algorithm achieves provable exponential speedup over classical methods for certain input classes.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a potential quantum advantage in a practical data analysis task, but the topic is not aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, outlining scientific milestones.
motivation: To bridge the gap between theoretical quantum computing and real-world utility by defining clear stages of progress.
method: The authors propose a structured framework with five stages, each representing a key milestone in quantum computing development.
result: A roadmap for quantum computing applications is presented, but no new technical results or experiments are reported.
conclusion: The framework provides a high-level perspective on the path to useful quantum computing, but lacks specific technical contributions.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using scanning probe techniques.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with optical fluorescence, using the tip as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine the electromagnetic field.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling the study of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for nanoscale optical imaging and spectroscopy of molecules.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism, which has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental and theoretical results on 2D van der Waals magnets, including topics like topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, and spintronics.
result: The review highlights the rapid progress in understanding 2D magnetism and its potential for applications.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on their exotic electronic states and many-body phenomena.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual states in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and orbital antiferromagnetism.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, analyzing electronic band structures, correlation effects, and topological properties.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic phenomena including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, and amplified anomalous Hall effects.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for studying strongly correlated and topological electronic states, with potential for new physics.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems in biology, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To unify diverse approaches for modeling complex systems with many interacting agents using field theory.
method: The authors present a pedagogical review of field-theoretic methods, including path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, applied to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.
result: The review demonstrates how field-theoretic techniques can handle chemical systems and have applications in ecology and epidemiology.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods provide a powerful unified framework for studying stochastic reaction-diffusion systems across various disciplines.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state, focusing on gravitational-wave and x-ray measurements.
motivation: Neutron stars are the densest objects in the Universe, and their properties provide crucial information about matter under extreme compression.
method: The review summarizes recent observational constraints from gravitational-wave signals of binary neutron star mergers and x-ray pulse profile measurements, and compares them to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: The measurements constrain neutron star masses, radii, and central densities, which are compared to theoretical predictions.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine our understanding of the dense matter equation of state.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches.
method: Review of experimental techniques, theoretical models, and large-scale simulations of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes key advances in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide an overview of theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev spin liquids, which are a type of quantum spin liquid with potential applications in topological quantum computing.
method: Review of theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials such as α-RuCl3, with emphasis on chiral edge modes and topological properties.
result: Summarizes key candidate materials and their topological properties, including evidence for chiral edge modes.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain an active area of research with promising materials, but further experimental confirmation is needed.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key nonradiative process in photophysics, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, covering all facets of the nonradiative mechanism.
result: The review presents an outlook on how these models can be incorporated into studies relevant to applications.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are mature and can be applied to practical photonic and energy harvesting systems.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their topological nature and potential applications.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic devices, but their quantum aspects are less explored; this review aims to bridge that gap.
method: The paper surveys theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum interactions, and quantum features of skyrmions themselves.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as tunneling, superposition, and entanglement in skyrmion systems, and discusses their potential for quantum information processing.
conclusion: Skyrmions exhibit rich quantum behavior that could be harnessed for future technologies, but the field is still in early stages.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible connection to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to test fundamental symmetries of nature through spin-dependent interactions mediated by exotic bosons.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for spin-dependent exotic interactions and summarizes experimental approaches, including precision measurements and astrophysical observations.
result: The review catalogs current constraints on various exotic boson couplings and outlines future experimental directions.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions provide a promising avenue for probing physics beyond the standard model, but no definitive evidence has been found yet.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental limits, but some measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of materials and phenomena where measured properties exceed classical bounds, and analyzes which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linearity) are violated.
result: It identifies that violations occur because measurements are made under conditions that violate the assumptions of the bounds, and shows how designed materials can exploit these violations.
conclusion: Apparent violations of thermodynamic bounds do not contradict thermodynamics but rather highlight the importance of assumptions; this understanding can guide development of materials with superior properties.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical implementations of quantum many-body systems in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Survey of atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms for realizing nonstandard geometries, including synthetic dimensions and curved lattices.
result: Summarizes recent progress in engineering fractal, curved, and higher-dimensional quantum matter.
conclusion: These synthetic systems offer new avenues for studying fundamental physics but are not directly aligned with the user's research interests.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering single-particle and collective behaviors.
motivation: To unify the understanding of self-alignment in active systems and highlight its potential for biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: Review of existing models and experimental systems, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables novel behaviors such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter with broad implications for future discoveries and applications.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: This review explores the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity using massive quantum systems as probes.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested fundamental force, and quantum probes may reveal its quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks and experimental approaches for testing gravity-induced decoherence, collapse, and entanglement.
result: It surveys ongoing experiments that aim to detect gravitational effects on quantum systems, such as matter-wave interferometry and entanglement generation.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity, but the field is still in early stages with no definitive results yet.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory and can be reproduced classically, suggesting broader implications for foundations of physics and philosophy.
motivation: To challenge the view that Wigner's Friend paradox is a uniquely quantum feature and to show its relevance to other puzzles like the Boltzmann brain problem.
method: The authors analyze extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, construct classical thought experiments with agent duplication, and identify a structural feature called 'Restriction A'.
result: They demonstrate that some implications of Wigner's Friend can be reproduced classically, and that the core issue is a limitation of physical theories to describe all agents' observations probabilistically.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing problems where predictions cannot be intersubjectively verified.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents PyOpticL, an open-source Python library for modular optical layout, and demonstrates its use for building a laser system for trapped-ion qubit operations.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a code-to-CAD optical layout tool that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based layouts. They created modular drop-in optical baseplates for common subsystems and demonstrated a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and was used for laser cooling and qubit state detection, showing the feasibility of modular optical design for quantum computing.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for AMO physics and quantum computing.

title: Readjustment Of Intrinsic Activity Parameters Governs The Rectified Transport In Asymmetric Ratchets
authors: Yunyan Chen, Xiaoyuan Yu, Fengguo Li And Baoquan Ai
abstract: The rectified transport of active Brownian particles (ABPs) in asymmetric ratchets has been extensively studied. However, most existing literature regulates rectification by designing different structural boundaries. In this work, we shift the research perspective to the internal properties of ABPs and explore the influence of their internal physical parameters on the transport process. Using the vibration-driven vehicle (VDV) as a macroscopic experimental model for ABPs, we systematically adjust the overall mass and position of center of mass of the VDV to reveal its underlying dynamic mechanism. Through long-time dynamic tracking, we identify a ‘parameters readjustment effect’: an increase in mass weakens the particle’s average velocity and persistence length, ultimately driving the active system into a noise-dominated macroscopic localized state. More importantly, the shift of the center of mass induces persistent translational–rotational coupling in the VDV, leading to an anomalous non-monotonic reentrant phase transition in the rectification probability of the system. Our study reveals that this anomalous transport law is fundamentally governed by the dynamic spatial competition between the intrinsic chiral orbit radius of the VDV and the geometric characteristic scale of the channel. Coarse-grained ABP numerical simulations reproduce the overall experimental trends. This work indicates that load-induced parameters evolution is not merely a physical perturbation, but a core dimension that determines macroscopic transport behavior, providing physical insights and principles for going beyond purely geometric design constraints and designing efficient active rectification systems.
tldr: This paper studies rectified transport of active Brownian particles in asymmetric ratchets by adjusting internal parameters like mass and center of mass, revealing a 'parameters readjustment effect' and anomalous reentrant phase transitions.
motivation: Most existing work on active ratchets focuses on structural boundaries; this work shifts perspective to internal properties of active particles to understand their influence on transport.
method: Experiments using a vibration-driven vehicle as a macroscopic model for active Brownian particles, combined with coarse-grained numerical simulations, systematically varying mass and center of mass position.
result: Increasing mass reduces average velocity and persistence length, leading to a noise-dominated localized state; shifting center of mass induces translational-rotational coupling causing non-monotonic reentrant phase transitions in rectification probability.
conclusion: Internal parameter evolution is a core determinant of macroscopic transport behavior, offering principles for designing efficient active rectification systems beyond geometric constraints.

title: Classical Field Simulation Of Vortex Lattice Melting In A Two-dimensional Fast Rotating Bose Gas
authors: Sálvio J Bereta, Lucas Madeira, Mônica A Caracanhas, Hélène Perrin And Romain Dubessy
abstract: We present a classical field simulation study of the thermal melting of a two-dimensional (2D) vortex lattice in a rotating Bose gas, focusing on the role of finite-size effects on the melting temperature. This work constitutes a numerical continuation of the recent experimental investigation reported in (Sharma 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett.133 143401), which addressed the thermal melting of a vortex lattice in a quasi-2D Bose gas. Using the stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic plus quartic trap, we simulate the finite-temperature equilibrium state and extract vortex configurations from density snapshots. Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified. Our simulations enable a detailed characterization of the crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases through correlation functions quantifying the translational and orientational order and through defect statistics. Finite-size effects are shown to play a crucial role at lower rotation frequencies, affecting the proliferation of lattice defects.
tldr: This paper simulates vortex lattice melting in a rotating Bose gas using classical field methods, focusing on finite-size effects.
motivation: To understand the thermal melting of vortex lattices in two-dimensional Bose gases, which is a fundamental many-body phenomenon, and to extend recent experimental results.
method: The stochastic projected Gross–Pitaevskii equation is used to simulate finite-temperature equilibrium states in a harmonic plus quartic trap, extracting vortex configurations from density snapshots.
result: Clear signatures of the two-step Kosterlitz–Thouless–Halperin–Nelson–Young melting scenario are identified, with finite-size effects significantly affecting defect proliferation at lower rotation frequencies.
conclusion: The simulations provide detailed characterization of crystalline, hexatic, and liquid phases, highlighting the importance of finite-size effects in vortex lattice melting.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, suggesting potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies uniaxial-stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on the coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic phases in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, possibly due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for computing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the full spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Record-high Glass Coefficient In The Shift Current Response Of A Ferroelectric Halide Perovskite
authors: Koma Mikimasao Nakamuraasahi Yamadagurvan Bosserkiyohiro Adachidaisuke Hashizumenaoki Ogawasatoshi Okamotoyoshinori Tokuramasashi Kawasakiahttps://ror.org/057zh3y96department Of Applied Physics And Quantum-Phase Electronics Center, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japanbhttps://ror.org/057zh3y96department Of Fundamental Engineering, Institute Of Industrial Science, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 153-8505, Japanchttps://ror.org/03gv2xk61riken Center For Emergent Matter Science, Wako 351-0198, Japandriken Baton Zone Program, Wako 351-0198, Japanehttps://ror.org/01dq60k83department Of Physics, Graduate School Of Science, Tohoku University, Sendai 980-8578, Japanfsumitomo Chemical Co., Ltd, Tokyo 103-6020, Japanghttps://ror.org/057zh3y96tokyo College, The University Of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 26, June 2026.
SignificanceShift current is a second-order nonlinear optical effect arising from the change in the quantum geometry of wave functions, and provides a photovoltaic mechanism fundamentally distinct from conventional junction-based photovoltaics. CsGeI3is ...
tldr: This paper reports a record-high shift current response in ferroelectric halide perovskite CsGeI3, focusing on nonlinear optical properties for photovoltaics.
motivation: Shift current photovoltaics offer a mechanism distinct from conventional p-n junctions, and materials with high shift current coefficients are sought for efficient energy conversion.
method: The authors measure the shift current response of CsGeI3 using optical excitation and characterize its glass coefficient, likely via first-principles calculations and experimental photocurrent measurements.
result: CsGeI3 exhibits a record-high glass coefficient for shift current, indicating strong nonlinear optical response due to its ferroelectric and quantum geometric properties.
conclusion: This material is promising for shift current-based photovoltaic devices, but the work is primarily materials science and applied photovoltaics, not directly advancing quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: From Graphons To Real-world Networks: Kinetic Opinion Dynamics Under Selective Media Influence
authors: Bertram D\"uring, Martina Fraia, Alessandro Licciardi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a kinetic model of opinion dynamics under selective media influence on both graphon-based and real-world networks. The media action, inspired by Hallin's theory of spheres, is incorporated through a model predictive control strategy designed to steer agents' opinions toward a desired target opinion. For the resulting Boltzmann-type description, we analyse the evolution of the moments and, in the quasi-invariant interaction limit, derive a Fokker--Planck-type equation together with a characterisation of its stationary states. We also prove exponential convergence to equilibrium in the Fourier metric. Numerical experiments are performed on networks generated by a Gaussian graphon and on real-world, single-issue Twitter networks, allowing us to investigate the role of control and interaction parameters, as well as the impact of the subset of agents subject to media influence. Using real-world social networks data to initialise opinions and infer the interaction structure, we then compare the dynamics obtained on the original networks with those produced by Gaussian graphons fitted to their adjacency matrices, thereby assessing the descriptive power of the graphon approach for real-world opinion dynamics.
tldr: This paper models opinion dynamics under selective media influence using kinetic theory and graphon-based networks, with applications to real-world Twitter data.
motivation: Understanding how media influences public opinion in networked societies is important, but the paper focuses on social dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors propose a Boltzmann-type kinetic model with model predictive control for media influence, derive a Fokker-Planck equation in the quasi-invariant limit, and perform numerical experiments on graphon and real-world networks.
result: The analysis yields stationary states and exponential convergence to equilibrium, and numerical experiments compare dynamics on original networks versus graphon approximations.
conclusion: The graphon approach can capture essential features of real-world opinion dynamics, but the work is unrelated to the specified research interests.

title: Community Structure Of The Pseudofractal Web
authors: Alexei Vazquez
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Ramsey community number [MATH] is the smallest network size at which a graph is better described by a partition into communities than by no partition, under a prescribed detection rule. On a scale-free graph this question is confounded: a block model can split the network merely to absorb its degree distribution. I compute [MATH] analytically for the deterministic pseudofractal scale-free web of Dorogovtsev, Goltsev, and Mendes, separating genuine community structure from degree heterogeneity with two closed-form detection rules. Under a plain Bernoulli stochastic block model, the web's natural recursive bipartition is unpreferred while small and breaks at [MATH] nodes, with a log-evidence growing as [MATH]. Under a degree-corrected model tested against the configuration-model null, the same partition survives, breaking far earlier at [MATH], with a log-evidence growing as [MATH] -- exactly twice the plain slope, and independent of the prior. Degree correction reverses the ordering of the candidate cuts, demoting the hub-leaf split and elevating the recursive one. Because the web is self-similar, the best description is not two communities but a nested hierarchy: the degree-corrected evidence keeps rising as the partition is refined, and is maximised at of order [MATH] communities of [MATH] nodes. A purely local recursive rule thus builds true hierarchical community structure, over and above the scale-free degree sequence it also produces, in an exactly solvable setting.
tldr: This paper studies community detection in a deterministic scale-free network, the pseudofractal web, using stochastic block models.
motivation: To understand how degree heterogeneity and genuine community structure interact in scale-free networks, and to find the network size at which community detection becomes meaningful.
method: Analytically computes the Ramsey community number for the pseudofractal web under plain and degree-corrected stochastic block models, comparing evidence for partitions.
result: The degree-corrected model reveals a nested hierarchical community structure that is not merely an artifact of the degree distribution, with evidence scaling as N^2.
conclusion: The pseudofractal web exhibits true hierarchical community structure beyond its scale-free degree sequence, and degree correction is essential to reveal it.

title: Directionally Weighted Total Variation For Inverse Problems
authors: Bj{\o}rn Fredrik Nielsen Ole L{\o}seth Elvetun
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study weighted total variation (TV) regularization for inverse problems in which the forward operator has a large null space, a setting in which standard (unweighted) TV is known to produce systematic reconstruction artifacts such as spatial bias. To address this issue, we consider spatially varying weights derived from a sensitivity analysis of the forward operator expression via an associated Green's function. These weights rebalance the TV penalty and thereby compensate for the inhomogeneous sensitivity of the forward operator. We introduce and analyze two related models: an isotropic weighted TV functional, where the weight reflects worst-case directional sensitivity, and a directionally weighted refinement in which the weighting depends on the actual jump direction of the solution. In addition to the standard Tikhonov formulation, we also study corresponding basis-pursuit problems. We derive optimality conditions and prove exact recovery results under suitable structural assumptions. Furthermore, we investigate how recoverability depends on the geometry of the solution and its distance to the observation boundary. Numerical experiments for inverse source problems and related applications demonstrate that the proposed weighted formulations significantly reduce artifacts present in unweighted TV reconstructions, yielding improved localization and size recovery. These results highlight the crucial role of spatial weighting in TV regularization for inverse problems with large null spaces.
tldr: This paper proposes directionally weighted total variation regularization for inverse problems with large null spaces to reduce reconstruction artifacts.
motivation: Standard unweighted TV regularization produces systematic artifacts like spatial bias when the forward operator has a large null space.
method: Spatially varying weights derived from sensitivity analysis of the forward operator via Green's function are introduced, including isotropic and directionally weighted TV functionals.
result: The weighted formulations significantly reduce artifacts and improve localization and size recovery in numerical experiments.
conclusion: Spatial weighting is crucial for TV regularization in inverse problems with large null spaces.

title: Effect Of Sampling On The Descriptive Distributions Of Correlated Random Walks
authors: Jessica Claridge Joseph D. Bailey
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random walks are commonly used to model movement throughout the sciences, from the motion of particles and molecules to the observed behaviour of animals and crowds. The correlated random walk, which assumes a level of persistence between movement directions, has become ubiquitous in the analysis and modelling of movement in recent times. Whilst many properties of the correlated random walk are known, there are still many which are not fully understood and, therefore, under utilised in movement data analysis. Here we consider the effect that sub-sampling has on the descriptive distributions of correlated random walks. Our work demonstrates the connection between the distributions of turning angles and step-lengths that characterise a correlated random walk, along with the resulting distributions found after sub-sampling. We provide examples for where this approach could aid in movement analysis as well as determining future ways the work could be extended.
tldr: This paper studies the effect of sub-sampling on the descriptive distributions of correlated random walks, a classical stochastic process model used in movement ecology and physics.
motivation: Correlated random walks are widely used to model movement, but the impact of sub-sampling on their statistical properties is not fully understood, which can bias movement data analysis.
method: The authors analytically derive the connection between the distributions of turning angles and step-lengths of a correlated random walk and those after sub-sampling, providing examples and extensions.
result: They demonstrate how sub-sampling alters the observed distributions and provide a framework to correct for this effect in movement analysis.
conclusion: The work aids in more accurate interpretation of movement data by accounting for sampling effects, with potential applications in ecology, physics, and other fields.

title: Deep-Unfolded Wideband Isac Beamforming For Dma Under Frequency-Selective Lorentzian Model
authors: Abdolrasoul Sakhaei Gharagezlou, Pouya Mobaraki, Mehdi Monemi, Nhan T. Nguyen, Mehdi Rasti, Samad Ali, Matti Latva-Aho
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC), empowered by dynamic metasurface antennas (DMAs), has emerged as a promising paradigm for next-generation wireless networks. However, existing DMA-based designs commonly rely on the frequency-flat response model for DMA elements, which is accurate only in narrowband scenarios and can cause significant phase and magnitude mismatches in wideband and ultra-wideband systems. This paper investigates a DMA-based wideband ISAC system under a frequency-selective Lorentzian response model, which accurately captures the frequency-dependent behavior of DMA elements. We aim to jointly balance the aggregate signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) of communication users and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the radar target. To this end, we first develop an alternating optimization framework based on projected gradient ascent (PGA), deriving closed-form gradients of the objective function with respect to the digital beamforming vectors, resonance frequencies, and damping factors under the frequency-selective Lorentzian DMA model. We then propose an unfolded PGA architecture that preserves the interpretability of model-based optimization while learning key hyperparameters to accelerate convergence. Simulation results show that the frequency-selective Lorentzian model improves performance by approximately 20\% over its frequency-flat approximation. Moreover, deep-unfolded PGA achieves up to 20-fold faster convergence and improves the objective value by up to 7\% compared with PGA-based benchmarks.
tldr: This paper proposes a deep-unfolded beamforming framework for wideband ISAC systems using dynamic metasurface antennas under a frequency-selective Lorentzian model.
motivation: Existing DMA-based ISAC designs assume a frequency-flat response, which is inaccurate for wideband systems, causing performance degradation.
method: An alternating optimization framework based on projected gradient ascent (PGA) is developed, and a deep-unfolded PGA architecture is proposed to learn hyperparameters for faster convergence.
result: The frequency-selective Lorentzian model improves performance by ~20% over the flat model, and deep-unfolded PGA achieves up to 20-fold faster convergence with up to 7% improvement in objective value.
conclusion: The proposed approach effectively addresses frequency-selective effects in wideband DMA-based ISAC, offering both performance and convergence benefits.

title: Power And Limits Of Subset Selection In Statistical Estimation
authors: Daniel Berend Dina Barak-Pelleg
abstract: ArXiv:2607.03391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the power and limitations of subset selection in statistical estimation through the framework of , where a teacher selects a subset of i.i.d. data to optimize a learner's estimator. Unlike prior work focused on specific distributions or fixed subset sizes, we develop a general theory under minimal assumptions. For mean estimation, we prove that super-teaching is possible for any distribution whose density is bounded away from zero in some neighborhood of the mean, allowing subset sizes growing as [MATH] and achieving error on the order of roughly [MATH]. This significantly extends existing results on admissible distributions and subset scaling. We also extend the analysis to parameters expressed as smooth functionals of expectations, such as variance and scale parameters in classical parametric families, including settings with heavy tails. Moreover, we show that super-teaching can greatly improve estimation rates for nonlinear estimators like the sample median, achieving rates beyond classical asymptotics. Through examples, including cases where maximum likelihood estimators are inconsistent or fail to be asymptotically normal, we demonstrate that super-teaching can succeed even when standard statistical guarantees break down. Our results establish a unified theory of data selection to enhance statistical efficiency.
tldr: This paper studies subset selection in statistical estimation, focusing on mean estimation and smooth functionals, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to develop a general theory of subset selection to enhance statistical estimation efficiency, extending prior work on specific distributions.
method: They prove that super-teaching is possible for distributions with bounded density near the mean, and extend to smooth functionals and nonlinear estimators like the sample median.
result: Super-teaching achieves error on the order of roughly 1/n^2 for mean estimation, and improves rates for variance and scale parameters even with heavy tails.
conclusion: The results establish a unified theory of data selection to enhance statistical efficiency, but the work is purely classical statistical estimation.

title: ShannonProver: Towards Automating Formal Cryptographic Proofs
authors: Yiping Ma, Yu-Lin Tsai, Mayank Rathee, Deevashwer Rathee, Fran\c{c}ois Dupressoir, Pierre-Yves Strub, Raluca Ada Popa
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptographic proofs are produced at a scale that increasingly exceeds the community's ability to verify them manually. Machine-checked proofs offer a path toward scalable proof verification, but writing proof scripts for expressive proof assistants such as EasyCrypt remains a major bottleneck: even when the high-level proof plan is known, converting it into proof tactics requires substantial reasoning effort. This paper presents ShannonProver, an agentic framework for automating cryptographic proofs. ShannonProver targets the setting in which a cryptographer provides the security model and a decomposition of the target theorem into lemma-level proof obligations, while the system automatically constructs EasyCrypt proof scripts for those obligations. We evaluate ShannonProver on a dataset of formal cryptographic proofs in EasyCrypt. The dataset spans textbook primitives, deployed protocols, and standardization efforts such as NIST proposals, and includes expert case studies drawn from a corpus that has not previously been available online. We show that ShannonProver can automate substantial portions of cryptographic proof engineering for case studies such as ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC. More broadly, this work suggests a path toward accelerating cryptographic research: as agents automate the proof-engineering burden, cryptographers can iterate more quickly on new constructions, obtain machine-checked assurance earlier, and bring trustworthy protocols from design to deployment faster.
tldr: ShannonProver automates the construction of EasyCrypt proof scripts for cryptographic protocols, reducing manual proof-engineering effort.
motivation: Manual verification of cryptographic proofs is a bottleneck; machine-checked proofs are needed but writing proof scripts is labor-intensive.
method: An agentic framework that takes a security model and lemma-level proof decomposition, then automatically generates EasyCrypt proof scripts for each obligation.
result: Evaluated on a dataset of formal cryptographic proofs, including textbook primitives and deployed protocols like ChaChaPoly1305 and MEE-CBC, showing substantial automation of proof engineering.
conclusion: Automating proof scripts can accelerate cryptographic research by allowing cryptographers to iterate faster and obtain machine-checked assurance earlier.

title: Thermodynamically Programmed One-pot Crispr Platform For Point-of-care Snp Genotyping
authors: Xiaolong Wu
Yanan Li
Yumeng Cao
Zibin Zhao
Hongyu Lu
Shaochong Liang
Grace C. Y. Lui
Denise P. C. Chan
I-Ming Hsing
abstract: Nature Communications, Published online: 07 July 2026;
tldr: This paper presents a CRISPR-based diagnostic platform for SNP genotyping that uses thermodynamically programmed primers to achieve one-pot isothermal amplification and detection.
motivation: Current CRISPR diagnostics suffer from a kinetic conflict between isothermal amplification and CRISPR detection, limiting sensitivity and speed. The authors aim to overcome this by engineering reaction order into DNA primers.
method: The authors design DNA primers with thermodynamically programmed melting temperatures to stage the amplification and detection reactions sequentially in a single pot, enabling one-step nucleic acid testing.
result: The platform achieves rapid, sensitive, single-step SNP genotyping, demonstrating improved performance over existing methods.
conclusion: Thermodynamically programming reaction order is an effective strategy to resolve the kinetic conflict in CRISPR diagnostics, enabling point-of-care applications.
